News.title: British soldier dies on holiday in Bali in 'every family’s worst nightmare'
News.content:
British soldier dies on holiday in Bali in 'every family’s worst nightmare'

British soldier Finlay John Perkins tragically died while on holiday with his friends and family in Bali - with a fundraiser launched to cover the cost of repatriating him to the UK

View 2 Images Finlay John Perkins sadly died earlier this month (Image: Jam Press)

A young British soldier has died while on holiday in Bali with his friends and family.

‌



Finlay John Perkins, known as Fin, passed away during a trip to the Indonesian island earlier this month. His devastated loved ones said the holiday should have been filled with laughter and treasured memories, but had instead become “every family’s worst nightmare”.

‌



Finlay’s cause of death has not been disclosed, although a fundraising appeal was launched to cover the significant cost of repatriating the soldier to the UK.

‌



Finlay, who is understood to have been from the Milton Keynes area, was remembered as a caring and selfless soldier who always put others first. More than £17,300 was raised towards a £20,000 target before donations were paused.

The appeal said: “It is with broken hearts that we share the sudden and tragic loss of Cfn Perkins, who passed away whilst on holiday with friends and family.

View 2 Images Finlay’s cause of death has not been disclosed (Image: Jam Press)

‌



Police probe as several motorists seen driving wrong way on M6 following crash READ MORE :

UK weather maps show 13 counties face heavy rain on Thursday with thunderstorms READ MORE :

“No one ever expects a trip filled with laughter, memories, and time spent with loved ones to end in such heartbreak. What should have been treasured moments together has instead become every family’s worst nightmare.”

Paying tribute to Finlay, the fundraiser added: “Cfn Perkins was more than a soldier, more than a colleague, and more than a friend.

“He was a son, a brother and a loyal friend to so many. He was the type of person who would put others before himself, offer a helping hand without hesitation, and bring a smile to those around him. His loss has left a void that can never truly be filled.”

‌



Finlay’s heartbroken family also announced his death in a Facebook post. They said: “We are incredibly devastated to share the news of the tragic loss of our son and little brother Fin.

“Fin was a character like no other, the most caring, selfless, determined and kind man who touched the hearts of many.

“There are no words for how much you’ll be missed, but your grandad and best friend, Aidan, have been reunited with an absolute legend. We will forever love you with all our hearts.”

‌



The Royal British Legion also paid tribute to Finlay and offered support to his family.

It said: “We’re very sorry to hear of the passing of Cfn Perkins, and send our deepest condolences to his family, comrades and loved ones. We’d also like to extend our practical support to his family – please do feel free to contact us to discuss what we can do to help.”

A funeral notice confirmed Finlay died on August 9.

Article continues below

Family and friends have been invited to escort him on foot from the old police station on Newport Pagnell High Street to St Peter and St Paul’s Church on September 10.

Donations in lieu of flowers can be made to the Jack the Lad charity.

News.title: Young people aged 18-24 are four times more likely to die after leaving care
News.content:
Young people aged 18-24 are four times more likely to die after leaving care

A review found 112 care leavers aged 18 to 24 died in 2025 and are dying at a high rate, with young people facing a dramatic drop in support as they reach adulthood

View 3 Images Care leavers aged 18 to 24 are up to four times more likely to die than others their age (Image: Getty Images/iStockphoto)

Young people leaving care are dying at a rate up to four times higher than others in their age group, a damning new report has revealed.

‌



A government-commissioned review found 112 deaths involving care leavers aged between 18 and 24 were reported in 2025 - an estimated rate of around 130 per 100,000. Tragically, 22 of those who died were just 18 - more deaths than at any other age covered by the review.

‌



The report said the figure was “strongly suggestive of the stark challenges and pressures” faced by young people as they leave care, when they can lose “significant levers of support”.

‌



Broadcaster Ashley John-Baptiste knows first-hand how isolating that transition can be. Ashley, who grew up in care and co-led the review alongside experienced social worker Clare Chamberlain, has recalled the daunting moment he left his foster family at 18 and found himself living alone in a council flat.

View 3 Images Ashley John-Baptise co-led the review (Image: Getty Images)

Beloved dog dies during grooming appointment with groomers only receiving small fine READ MORE :

Cat rescued from car engine finally freed after eight-hour ordeal READ MORE :

Ashley told LBC: “At 18 years old, I was placed into a council flat, and I still remember that moment of having to leave my foster family and live alone in this council flat.

‌



“Couldn’t afford a bed frame, so I had to sleep on the living room floor on a mattress. And being that first night in that flat on that mattress, just the deep sense of isolation and vulnerability.”

His experience reflects the loneliness and vulnerability uncovered among some of the young people whose deaths were examined.

The report described those who died as young people “at the height of vulnerability who were isolated and often very lonely”. It added: “On reaching 18, they faced a dramatic drop in support and received inconsistent and, at times, inadequate help from both children’s and adults’ services. They were alone, with no safety net and with catastrophic consequences.”

‌



More than a third of the 112 care leavers who died - 40 young people - were thought to have taken their own lives. The report said the potential suicide rate among care leavers was five times higher than in the general population.

Overall, it found young care leavers aged between 18 and 24 were dying at an estimated rate “about three to four times higher than the death rate in the general population”.

Ashley, who has written a book about his childhood in care, branded it a “national tragedy that so many care-experienced young people are dying so early in life” and described the stories he heard as “heart-breaking”. He said: “These young lives ended far too soon.”

‌



View 3 Images The report described those who died as young people “at the height of vulnerability who were isolated and often very lonely”. (Image: Getty Images)

The shocking findings come as the Government moves to increase the help available to young people after they leave care.

£25million has been announced this year for the Staying Close programme, which aims to help care leavers up to the age of 25 stay in settled accommodation rather than being moved on alone at 18. Those receiving support are also given a named adult who stays in touch and can help with things such as accessing healthcare, education and employment.

‌



The programme currently operates in 47 local areas across England, but the Government plans to roll it out nationwide by 2029.

Further changes will come into force from September 30, requiring local authorities to publish how they will support young people leaving care as they move towards independent living.

From the same date, a young person who has left care can no longer be found intentionally homeless.

Article continues below

When life is difficult, Samaritans are available day or night, 365 days a year. You can call them for free on 116 123 or visit samaritans.org

News.title: Driver amazed to see wallaby hopping along street in Cornwall
News.content:
Driver amazed to see wallaby hopping along street in Cornwall

Pasty shop owner Scot Weller was driving into a town in Cornwall when he spotted the animal hopping across the road - and soon realised it was a wallaby

View 2 Images A wallaby was spotted by a surprised driver in Cornwall (Image: Scot Weller / SWNS)

A driver has told of the bizarre moment he spotted a wallaby hopping around a town in Cornwall.

‌



Pasty shop owner Scot Weller was driving into Liskeard when he saw what he believed at first to be a dog in the road ahead.

‌



He said the animal was hopping along the road in front of him as he drove to work. Feeling in a protective mood, he decided to follow it, as there were several cars behind him and he was worried it could be hit.

‌



The animal then made its way onto the pavement and stopped - and it was only then that Mr Weller realised that it was in fact a wallaby. He said: "I realised it was hopping and that it was a wallaby on the loose."

Exotic pet ownership SURGES in UK with more than 300 dangerous big cats living in regular homes READ MORE :

Cat rescued from car engine finally freed after eight-hour ordeal READ MORE :

View 2 Images Scot Weller was driving into Liskeard when he saw what he initially thought was a dog (Image: Scot Weller / SWNS)

Scot, owner of Original Cornish Pasties, pulled up alongside the escaped marsupial and said: "Hello, you’re not from around here, are you?" A few seconds later, the escaped marsupial disappeared down a side road towards the local Co-op.

‌



"It was a bit sad that he was out there on his own, as there can’t have been much for it to eat because of the heatwave we’ve been having," Scot said. "I just thought, ‘Poor thing, he’s lost.’"

He reported the sighting to police via 101, although the call handler initially had some trouble understanding what he was reporting. He said: "I told her, ‘There’s a wallaby hopping up the street,’ and she replied, ‘The Australian animal, like a small kangaroo? Right, OK.’"

The wallaby has reportedly been sighted elsewhere in Liskeard. A member of staff at the leisure centre is also said to have spotted it at the weekend in the secondary school playing fields.

‌



A Devon and Cornwall Police spokesperson said that the animal had disappeared by the time officers arrived. They said: "We were called to a report of a wallaby seen on Dean Street, Liskeard, shortly before 6am today, August 24. Officers carried out an area search but did not locate the animal."

Wallabies are an increasingly common sight in the British countryside, with a growing number of the marsupials spotted in fields, grasslands and woods up and down the country.

Last month, a wallaby was spotted by a driver in north Devon - the latest sighting of an animal thought to have been roaming around the county for at least three years.

‌



Danny Reynolds, a partner at Exmoor Zoo, said staff have known about the mysterious wallaby for years. He told Devon Live: "As far I’m aware, we are not missing a wallaby. But we do know about this one. It’s been living in the wild for about three years.

"We’ve made numerous attempts to capture it and every single time, even with a team of 15 people, it’s beaten us. You see it once and then you don’t see it again for months. It’s a bit like the Exmoor Beast, except this one poses for the occasional photo."

Breeding populations have previously been found in the Peak District and the Scottish islands, with the creatures well suited to the rugged, hilly terrain.

Article continues below

Many of those currently around are thought to have escaped zoos or private collections, though there have been a few deliberate introductions over the past few decades.

News.title: Dad's house rammed before son died in A66 crash
News.content:
A house rammed by a car before the fatal A66 crash in Middlesbrough belonged to the father of a teenager who died in the incident.

Cole Worthy was one of five young men in a Volkswagen Passat travelling the wrong way down the A66 who were killed when it hit a Cleveland Police armed response vehicle in the early hours of Saturday, also killing two police officers.

The force said that morning, and the previous night, it had received multiple reports of two cars driving dangerously around the town and a Volvo XC60, believed to be linked to the Passat, was seen ramming properties in the town.

There is no suggestion the 17-year-old's father was involved in criminal activity.

PC Tom Clough, 38, and PC Matthew Blades, 37, died in the crash, as did Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jacob Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18, Theo Rae, 17, and 17-year-old Cole Robert Worthy.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct said officers had been pursuing the Passat for almost seven minutes after it was connected to earlier alleged criminal activity, but the pursuit was abandoned 10 seconds before the crash when it turned on to the dual carriageway.

Both vehicles were operating with cloned number plates but were picked up by automated number plate recognition technology.

The red bricked semi-detached house a quiet residential street in Acklam hit by the Volvo is significantly damaged.

The downstairs bay window has been smashed, with bricks scattered beneath it, and an upstairs bedroom window has been broken also.

The BBC understands the car rammed the property in the early hours of Saturday and Cole and the four other young men killed in the crash on the A66 set out in a VW Passat a short time later.

Neighbours did not want to be identified but one described hearing loud bangs at around two in the morning on Saturday. Another said the street had been full of police all weekend.

News.title: Trump may hope an 'economic onslaught' will pressure Iran - its leaders are betting otherwise
News.content:
The US says it has launched an "economic onslaught against Iran's financial connections around the globe". Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said sanctions included digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping. Any nation financially partnering with Iran would be isolated.

However, Bessent's announcement of what he termed an "economic D-Day" may have sounded more dramatic in Washington than in Tehran.

Shortly after the announcement, Iran's Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh called it "the same old talk" and said Iran was ready for "every scenario". He said Tehran had expected the measures and had plans to deal with them.

His reaction points to the main question Iranian leaders are likely to be asking: What can the US do now that it has not already tried?

Bessent has threatened wider secondary sanctions against countries, banks and companies that continue doing business with Iran. But the basic policy is not new. Iran has faced US sanctions for years, including penalties against foreign companies trading with it.

What matters to Tehran is whether Washington can enforce sanctions more widely than before.

The US blockade has already made a difference. It has reduced Iran's ability to export as much oil by sea as it did before and made it harder to import goods and equipment. Iran has long land borders with seven countries and years of experience using them to bypass sanctions. But land routes cannot easily replace trade by sea, especially oil exports.

The pressure could therefore become much more serious if Washington manages to close channels that survived previous sanctions, particularly those involving China and Iran's neighbours. That is a big ask. China's foreign ministry said on Tuesday that it firmly opposed the sanctions, calling them illegal.

If the sanctions fail, Bessent's announcement could strengthen those inside Iran who oppose a deal with the US.

They could argue that Washington has returned to economic pressure because its other choices are limited. A new military campaign carries risks, while years of sanctions have failed to force Iran to accept US demands.

Washington has also left little room for diplomacy.

Although Pakistan and other mediators are still trying to revive talks, the US has not ruled out further strikes. The renewed threats could weaken Iranian officials who favour a deal.

News.title: Man dies in crash after police pursuit
News.content:
A man has died and two women have been injured in a crash after a police pursuit near Stratford-upon-Avon.

Officers tried to stop a black Audi on Birmingham Road shortly before 17:30 BST on Monday but the driver failed to pull over, Warwickshire Police said.

A pursuit began and 15 minutes later the Audi crashed into a white Ford Puma, the force added, with the Audi's male driver confirmed dead at the scene by paramedics.

The driver of the Ford, a woman, was seriously injured and remains in hospital in critical condition, while injuries to a second woman - her passenger - were serious but not believed to be life-threatening. An investigation by the police watchdog is under way.

Officers said after failing to stop, the Audi made off in the direction of the A46 before travelling back towards Stratford on the A439 Warwick Road where the crash occurred.

A number of other cars were damaged during the pursuit, police said.

Warwick Road was closed on Monday from the Marraway roundabout to its junction with Ingon Lane and Sand Barn Lane, with the stretch remaining shut on Tuesday morning.

It has since reopened.

News.title: Yellow weather warnings issued as thunderstorms and flooding forecast
News.content:
Yellow weather warnings have been issued by the Met Office as heavy rain and thunderstorms are forecast to break out over parts of the UK later this week.

The warnings span Wednesday and Thursday and include parts of east Wales, the Midlands, northern England, East Anglia and southern England - including London.

It is likely to be the one of the most widespread outbreaks of heavy rain across southern and central parts of the UK this summer.

While good news for regions plagued by drought, significant accumulations could lead to flash flooding where the ground is too dry and hard to absorb the downpours. Lightning, large hail and gusty winds are also possible.

News.title: Young people leaving care have death rate four times higher than national average
News.content:
Young adults who have left care have a death rate around four times higher than the general population, a new review, external shows.

Often left alone "with no safety net," the report says the consequences can be catastrophic.

On turning 18, people leaving care in England often lose "significant levers of support", the Government-commissioned report concluded, as it warned the so-called "care cliff" must be addressed.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4 Today, report co-author and broadcaster Ashley John-Baptiste, who grew up in care, called the deaths a national tragedy.

There were 112 deaths of care leavers aged 18 to 24 notified in 2025, which the review said equalled about 130 deaths per 100,000 care leavers.

John-Baptiste recalled his own experience of turning 18 and moving out of the last of four foster homes he'd lived in.

"I was made to live alone and work out how to be an adult," he said.

Unable to afford a bed frame, he says he slept on a mattress on the floor of his council flat and felt a deep sense of abandonment and isolation.

News.title: US judge rejects Ghislaine Maxwell's 'frivolous' appeal against conviction
News.content:
Ghislaine Maxwell's latest bid to overturn her sex trafficking conviction has been rejected by a US judge, who dismissed her claims as "frivolous" and "meritless".

The 64-year-old is serving a 20-year prison sentence for her role in procuring girls for the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein after being found guilty in December 2021.

Maxwell had appealed against her five felony convictions, claiming her constitutional rights had been "violated in multiple respects".

But a New York judge flatly rejected the appeal, describing it as "lengthy and rambling".

Maxwell said Epstein-related documents released by the US Justice Department earlier this year supported her case that she had been wrongly convicted.

But the judge ruled that "far from exculpating her, it incriminates her or reinforces the correctness" of her conviction.

The judge warned Maxwell against making further appeals, saying it "would not be taken in good faith" by the court.

News.title: Boy, 3, injured in crocodile attack returns home from hospital
News.content:
A three-year-old boy who was seriously injured in a crocodile enclosure has been discharged from hospital and is settling back in at home, his family has said.

The child returned home "a few weeks ago" and is "happy to be home, playing with his toys, sleeping in his own bed and being a big brother", his parents said in an update posted online.

The boy was visiting Johnsons of Old Hurst near Huntingdon, Cambridgeshire, with his family on 18 June when he was attacked by at least one of the animals.

In an update shared on a fundraising page on Monday, the boy's family said it was "nice to have us all back together in the comfort of our own home".

Cambridgeshire Police arrested and bailed a 30-year-old man from Norfolk on suspicion of attempted murder after the incident.

News.title: Kate Hudson to make How to Lose a Guy in 10 Days sequel, 23 years on
News.content:
The movie grossed nearly $180m worldwide at the box office at the time.

The yellow silk Carolina Herrera dress Hudson wore near the end of the film also became a much talked-about piece of modern cinema fashion.

The star's most recent film role was in 2025's Song Sung Blue, which earned her a second Oscar nomination, following her first nod for Almost Famous back in 2001.

McConaughey's films include Dallas Buyer's Club, which won him an Oscar in 2014, The Wedding Planner and Magic Mike. He also appeared in 2008 movie Fool's Gold alongside Hudson.

Representatives for Hudson and McConaughey have been contacted for comment.

The new film would be the latest in a trend for nostalgic sequels in Hollywood, following The Devil Wears Prada 2 - which came 20 years after the original and also featured a magazine employee called Andy (played by Anne Hathaway).

In 2024, McConaughey told People magazine about his first meeting with Hudson before filming How to Lose a Guy in 10 Days.

"Immediately, we were comfortable with each other, and we jacked with each other, and we busted each other's chops, and we laughed a lot," he recalled.

"There was a bit of rock and roll exchange, like, 'Oh, this could be some heavyweight fun.' And I think that's why I was cast, and that's why, for whatever extent, it worked."

News.title: More than 70,000 social and affordable homes to be built across England over 10 years
News.content:
Ministers have announced where more than 70,000 social and affordable homes will be built in England over the next 10 years as part of an initial allocation of almost Â£10bn in a bid to address the housing crisis.

Funding has been granted to Greater Manchester, the West Midlands, West Yorkshire, South Yorkshire, North East England, and Liverpool. An additional Â£6bn was previously announced for London.

It is the first part of a wider plan to build 300,000 social and affordable homes, under the government's Â£39bn social housebuilding programme.

Housing charities welcomed the news but said it was still not enough to meet demand, while the Conservatives said it was an "unfunded spending commitment".

Social housing provides affordable homes at a low cost, managed by social landlords. It includes affordable rented properties as well as low-cost home ownership, such as shared ownership, and can be provided by local authorities and housing associations.

Earlier this year, before he became prime minister, Andy Burnham had called for the entire Â£39bn affordable housing budget for England to be spent on homes for social rent - which means the cost of the unit is about half that of market rents, and there are strict criteria for who can apply for it.

"I would actually devote all of it to social housing," Burnham told The Social Housing Podcast in May.

But of the new homes announced on Monday, 60% would be for social rent.

Housing Minister Matthew Pennycook told BBC Breakfast he did not accept Burnham had failed to meet his previous commitment, saying the government had taken a "pragmatic approach" and wants to "get money out the door".

He said the next tranche of funding would be more focused on council houses - which are usually also classed as homes for social rent.

It is understood ministers decided against giving councils more of the funding announced in the first tranche because they did not believe councils would be in a position to build the required number of social homes.

News.title: Burnham refuses to rule out tax rises in autumn Budget
News.content:
Andy Burnham has refused to rule out tax rises in the upcoming autumn Budget, saying he "won't be unrealistic" about the "challenging" state of public finances.

The prime minister said he would take a "careful approach" to the economy, and defended his previously announced cost of living pledges as funded spending commitments.

Burnham became prime minister in July promising to give people breathing space and help with the cost of living, but questions remain over how major policies such as social care reforms will be funded.

Experts have previously warned that he and Chancellor John Healey will have little financial room to manoeuvre in their first Budget on 28 October.

Speaking during his first visit to Ukraine, Burnham said the policies announced so far including capping bus fares at Â£2 and cutting VAT on household electricity bills were "the first steps that I've felt able to make", and were doable because he was able to reprioritise funding from elsewhere.

"I took the decision early on that digital ID wasn't the top priority for now. And so we've reprioritised funding to other priorities," he said in an interview with ITV.

Asked if the public needed to accept some of the new policies would have to be paid for in tax rises, Burnham said they wouldn't necessarily have to accept that.

Pushed on whether he would need to raise taxes to cover spending gaps, he said: "I will always take a careful approach to things. I ran Greater Manchester for 10 years and we ran a very tight ship with rock solid finances.

"Nothing will change as I come into this role as prime minister. I won't take risks with people's jobs or their livelihoods or their family finances.

"I will try to help them in whatever way I can, I have already done some things that will help them."

Burnham previously told the BBC he accepts his earlier announcements aimed at tackling the cost of living are not enough on their own and hinted at further support.

Speaking during his first official overseas visit on Monday, he said while he would do what he could, "I won't be unrealistic and people really need to understand that.

"We are in a challenging position, whatever I do will be carefully thought through, it will be funded and there will be more to come as we go into the autumn."

Last week official figures showed the the government borrowed more than expected in July, despite a record month for income tax receipts.

Inflation also reached a four-month high of 2.9% in July and is expected to rise further due to the ongoing impact of the Iran war, which has hit energy prices and fuel costs.

Experts have warned Burnham and Healey that they need to either raise taxes or cut spending elsewhere as pressure on the public finances has left no room for extra borrowing.

Both the prime minister and chancellor have vowed to stick to the fiscal rules set by former chancellor Rachel Reeves.

The rules are designed to ensure day-to-day spending is funded through tax revenue by the end of the Parliament, and to reduce debt as a proportion of GDP.

Rain Newton-Smith, chief executive of the Confederation of British Industry, said business owners wanted to create opportunities for young people but "the cost of employing people has gone up so much".

"The business leaders I speak to say that the cost of doing business has gone up so much that it's holding them back from creating opportunities," she told the Today programme.

She said targeted support for businesses would create "more growth and more opportunities that saves money for the government and ultimately leads to higher tax receipts".

News.title: Legendary rugby league winger Boston dies aged 92
News.content:
Rugby league legend Sir Billy Boston has died aged 92.

Last year, he became the first player in rugby league's 130-year history to receive a knighthood.

Born in Cardiff in 1934, Boston grew up playing union but - overlooked by his home club - came to the attention of rugby league scouts while on national service in the north of England, signing for Wigan in 1953 as a 19-year-old.

Despite having played just a handful of games in league, the young winger's talent was quickly evident and Boston was picked for the 1954 Great Britain side that went to Australia and New Zealand - becoming the first black British player to tour down under.

He reached the 100-try milestone in just 68 matches after his switch from union.

Boston's scoring ratio is extraordinary, claiming 478 tries in 488 games for Wigan and helping them win three Challenge Cups and the Championship.

News.title: 'We just want to get home' - dozens stranded in Tunisia after cancelled Belfast flight
News.content:
Dozens of people from Northern Ireland have been left stranded in Tunisia after their EasyJet flight back to Belfast was cancelled and the airline told them it had no other flights available for another 10 days.

A number of people have scrambled for alternative journeys back to Northern Ireland, with one man saying he has spent more than Â£4,000 to get his family of five home.

Some told BBC News NI of passengers running out of medication in the days since the cancellation on Saturday, while others criticised EasyJet over a lack of support and communication.

EasyJet has said it is operating an additional direct flight to Belfast on Tuesday night, and that it was "very sorry" for the inconvenience.

BBC News NI understands more than 100 people were booked onto the cancelled flight that was due to leave Enfidha-Hamamet Airport three days ago.

Stuart McCartney, from Dromore, County Down, said he had spent thousands on accommodation and flights to get his family home via a flight to Brussels.

"I'm willing to pay Â£4,000 to get us home, if needs be, and then battle for reimbursement if I have to after that," he said.

"But we shouldn't have to pay. My holiday was a fraction of what I'm paying to get home right now."

McCartney said EasyJet provided two nights of accommodation but then told the family to find alternative accommodation for the rest of the delay.

He said his mother Katherine, who accompanied his wife and children on the trip, relies on heart medication and they have had to keep a close eye on her remaining supply as the delay continued.

An EasyJet spokesperson said they were "very sorry" that the flight had been cancelled and that the company "have been doing everything we can to support Mr McCartney, providing hotel accommodation and meals and we will be reimbursing expenses that may have been incurred".

Another woman, Martine Murray, said she had run out of an inhaler to treat her COPD (Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease) and is anxious to get home to her mother, who is seriously ill.

Chloe McGinty, a student from County Donegal, said it had been "an absolute nightmare".

News.title: Andrew Tate exaggerates and did not own supercars in photos, his lawyers say
News.content:
Controversial influencer Andrew Tate portrays himself as "uberwealthy" but did not own cars and a yacht featured on his social media and exaggerated his lifestyle for online attention, his legal representatives have said.

Tate and his brother Tristan are currently being held in a Florida jail but are seeking release on bail while they await the outcome of extradition proceedings.

They were arrested last month after British prosecutors unveiled new charges including alleged sexual offences against them, which both men deny.

Prosecutors have argued the Tates are a "flight risk", citing the brothers' past statements about their wealth and influence and having multiple identities to evade the law.

In a legal submission to the court, the brothers' legal representatives said the Tates' business model "depends on online attention".

"The outrageousness of the posts by them and about them is the point. The more hyperbolic and outlandish the post, the more likely it will generate views and likes, which in turn generates income. In short, they are playing a role," it says.

At times Andrew Tate has also exaggerated and used hyperbole for "comedic effect" with no intention to be taken seriously, the submission argues.

"The government alleges that the Tates are a risk of flight based on their social media claims that they are 'self-proclaimed billionaires' who own 'high-end vehicles, private jets, and a custom $50-million-dollar superyacht and have unrestricted access to traditional funds, cryptocurrency, and bitcoin,'" it says.

"But the government has not established these grandiose claims are true," it adds.

News.title: Man guilty of killing student after fake Rolex row
News.content:
At about 17:00 GMT on the night he died, Oladipo left his girlfriend's flat carrying a plastic bag of leftover snacks and was on the phone to her while he walked back to his accommodation nearby to watch football.

But outside the De Montfort University's Innovation Centre Innovation Centre, he was met by Dennis who was captured on CCTV walking up and down in the "busy" area.

"It took less than 30 seconds for the two men to come together, to struggle and for the defendant to leave," Osborne told the court.

The court was told Oladipo's girlfriend heard him say "why did you come up and stab me?" over the phone before asking for her to call the ambulance.

A post-mortem examination showed he had suffered six wounds, five to the chest including one which penetrated his heart, and one to his thumb.

Despite being taken to the Leicester Royal Infirmary, he was pronounced dead just over an hour after the stabbing, which took place near the DMU campus.

Giving evidence in his defence on Wednesday, Dennis said he was "fearful" for his life when Oladipo approached him with a knife, adding he was "wrestling" to prevent the 20-year-old from stabbing him.

In cross-examination, prosecutor Jane Osborne KC asked if Dennis knew he had stabbed Oladipo, to which he replied: "I didn't know and I didn't know he was hurt, and I didn't intend to cause any serious harm."

Jurors were shown CCTV footage of Oladipo and Dennis walking towards each other, with Osborne suggesting Dennis used his hands to open a folding knife.

Dennis denied the suggestion he had a knife in his possession, and said he did not leave his accommodation with one.

Addressing Dennis, the prosecutor said there was "bad feeling" between Dennis and Oladipo - and suggested Dennis left his accommodation with a knife "to settle it".

News.title: Man convicted after being caught on CCTV upskirting girl in shopping centre
News.content:
A man has pleaded guilty to filming beneath a young girl's skirt in a shopping centre before running off and later being tracked down on CCTV.

Alex Allegretto, 39, admitted the offence of operating a mobile phone beneath the clothing of another person for the purpose of obtaining sexual gratification.

Police were called to St David's 2 shopping centre on the morning of 7 July after a mother reported Allegretto, who was unknown to them, for upskirting her daughter.

He was caught on CCTV heading back to his car and was later arrested for voyeurism at his home in Maesteg, in Bridgend County Borough.

Allegretto was sentenced at Cardiff Magistrates' Court on 5 August.

The CCTV footage shows Allegretto sat on a bench before quickly walking up behind the victim and her mum in the busy shopping centre and putting his phone by her legs before running away.

Sgt Luis Antony, from South Wales Police, said the victim had continued to be impacted by the incident.

"She is worried about people walking behind her and is anxious when out and about," he added.

Antony said that "nobody should be subjected to this kind of offence".

"The footage clearly shows Alex Allegretto's intentions and what he did to this young girl while she was innocently out shopping with her mother," he added.

"We hope the outcome at court provides some comfort to her and allows her to rebuild her confidence."

The court heard that Allegretto must be registered with the police in accordance with the Sexual Offences Act 2003 , externalfor five years.

He must also do 140 hours of unpaid work, complete rehabilitation activity requirements and pay a financial penalty of Â£199.

News.title: New 10p coin enters circulation - will you spot one?
News.content:
Something new might appear in your change when you pay in cash from now on: a 10p coin featuring the portrait of King Charles and the world's largest grouse.

Sufficient demand for the coins mean newly-minted 10p pieces are entering circulation for the first time for about four years, this time with a new design.

The Royal Mint says shoppers and collectors should discover the coins, which were minted and dated in 2023 and 2026, across the country.

The reverse side of the coin depicts an image of the capercaillie which is found in a small part of Scotland and threatened with extinction.

The redesigned suite of coins to celebrate the King's love of the natural world were unveiled in October 2023 by The Royal Mint.

The tails side of every newly-minted coin from the 1p to the Â£2 now features the country's flora and fauna - from bees to an oak tree leaf.

Coins in circulation in the UK carrying the portrait of King Charles have so far been limited to the 5p, 50p and Â£1.

Old coins with the image of the late Queen Elizabeth II can still be used, so the new coins are only struck in response to demand.

That is why, with 1.4 billion 10p coins in circulation, there has been no need for the new 10p to be released until now by The Royal Mint.

Now. 600,000 of these coins, dated 2023, and 6.5 million dated 2026 have been released to banks and post offices nationwide.

However, King Charles III coins still only represent about 1% of the 24.1 billion coins in circulation across the UK, making any new ones highly sought after by seasoned numismatists and new coin collectors.

Christopher McDonald has opened up about the heartbreak he felt when his fiancée Geena Davis left him to be with Jeff Goldblum.

During a recent career retrospective for the SAG-AFTRA Foundation, McDonald spoke about the end of his engagement to Davis in the mid-1980s.

“Geena Davis and I were engaged to be married for about five weeks and she fell in love with Jeff Goldblum doing her first movie over there in Europe,” McDonald shared. Davis and Goldblum were filming Transylvania 6-5000 at the time.

“And I don’t blame him,” McDonald continued. “She’s stunningly beautiful and everything like that, but you know, what happens on sets — things sometimes happen.

“But I was broken,” he continued.

open image in gallery Christopher McDonald (left) has opened up about his fiancee Geena Davis leaving him for Jeff Goldblum ( Getty )

“I was doing Hamlet at the time, playing Laertes, and I had another three weeks to finish and then I was going to go over and join her,” McDonald said. “So I got the bad news from Ed Begley. He did me that solid.

“I mean I was really, really devastated.”

Davis and Goldblum went on to marry in 1987 before filing for divorce in 1990, citing irreconcilable differences.

McDonald and Davis then reconnected while working on the 1991 film Thelma & Louise.

He recalled: “It’s literally five years later and [Davis] said to [Director Ridley Scott], ‘Who’d you get to play my husband?’ and he said, ‘Oh, you’ll love him, he’s tall, he’s funny, uh .... what’s his name? Chris McDonald,’ and then she said, ‘I used to go with him,’ and he said, ‘Even better, perfect!’”

McDonald said he and Davis met for lunch and “hugged it out.”

open image in gallery McDonald and Davis reconnected while working on the 1991 film ‘Thelma and Louise’ ( MGM )

“We had a really lovely afternoon and then we did what I think is probably the most ironic thing in the world: Let's do wedding pictures and put them around the house for the set decorators,” he said. “We did all that, it turned out great and we’re dear friends now.”

For her part, Davis wrote about the overlap in the relationships in her 2022 memoir Dying of Politeness.

“When I left for the movie, I was living with-and engaged to—one of the most wonderful men I’ve ever known, the actor Christopher McDonald. He was and is a truly beautiful person,” she wrote. “And I broke his heart to be with Jeff, I’m ashamed to say. He didn’t deserve that at all, and this dear man eventually forgave me, for which I will always be grateful.”

McDonald went on to marry Lupe Gidley in 1992. They share four children.

After divorcing Goldblum, Davis went on to marry Renny Harlin from 1993 to 1998 and plastic surgeon Reza Jarrahy from 2001 to 2021. She shares three children with Jarrahy.

Goldblum married Emilie Livingston in 2014. They share two children.

As summer vacations and late nights end, it is time to set morning school alarms again.

Adequate rest ensures students remain attentive and focused during class. Experts advise easing children back into a routine as the start of the new academic year approaches.

"We don't say ‘ get good sleep ’ just because," said pediatrician Dr. Gabrina Dixon with Children's National Hospital. "It really helps kids learn and it helps them function throughout the day."

Sleep requirements change as children grow older. Preschoolers should receive up to 13 hours of rest. Tweens need nine to 12 hours, while teenagers function best with eight to 10 hours of sleep.

open image in gallery Experts advise easing children back into a routine as the start of the new academic year approaches ( Getty Images )

Set an earlier bedtime

Late summer routines filled with sleepovers, movie marathons, and long flights frequently cause children's bedtimes to slide. To reset schedules for the return to school, specialists recommend establishing earlier sleep times a week or two in advance, or shifting bedtime back in 15- to 30-minute increments each night.

Parents should avoid serving heavy meals close to bedtime and cut off screens two hours before sleep. Replacing devices with soothing activities, like a warm shower or a bedtime story, helps ease the transition to sleep.

"You're trying to take the cognitive load off your mind," said Dr. Nitun Verma, a spokesperson for the American Academy of Sleep Medicine. "It would be like if you're driving, you're slowly letting go of the gas pedal."

Every family can tailor their approach. Nikkya Hargrove moves her twin daughters' bedtime up by 30 minutes in the final week before school resumes.

When her children bargain for a few extra minutes to read, Hargrove encourages the conversation as a way for them to practice self-advocacy. She also notes that a tired morning after staying up late offers its own practical lesson.

"If they're groggy and they don't like how they feel, then they know, ‘OK, I have to go to bed earlier,’" said Hargrove, an author and independent bookstore owner from Connecticut.

To start the next day, getting natural daylight by sitting near a window or going outdoors helps prompt the brain to wake up, Verma added.

Squash back-to-school sleep anxiety

How well a child sleeps is just as critical as how many hours they spend in bed. Anxiety about the start of the term can make it difficult for children to fall asleep, regardless of how early they go to bed.

Dixon recommends that parents speak directly with their children to identify specific worries, whether it involves starting at a new school or making friends. Practicing potentially stressful situations before the academic year begins—such as touring the building or attending an open house to meet peers—can make those experiences feel less daunting.

Although chaotic schedules late in the summer can make early preparation challenging, sleep specialists note that children will eventually adapt. Parents are encouraged to simply manage what they can, keeping in mind that adults are also adjusting to the shift in routine.

"I always say, 'Take a deep breath, it'll be OK,'" Dixon said. "And just start that schedule."

News.title: Judge rejects Ghislaine Maxwell’s ‘frivolous’ attempt to throw out trafficking convictions after Epstein files release
News.content:

A federal judge has rejected Ghislaine Maxwell’s “lengthy and rambling” attempt to throw out her sex trafficking convictions after she claimed new evidence released by the Department of Justice in connection with her associate Jeffrey Epstein proved her rights at trial and sentencing were violated.

“Maxwell’s claims are all meritless and all or almost all are frivolous,” according to Tuesday’s order from New York District Judge Paul Engelmayer.

Most of her arguments, which she filed herself while imprisoned, were already turned down in appeals courts, while the alleged “new” evidence from the Justice Department’s Epstein files are “largely irrelevant" to her case, the judge said.

“On the contrary, to the extent it is relevant, far from exculpating her, it incriminates her or reinforces the correctness of the legal rulings Maxwell challenges,” he added.

Maxwell, who is now representing herself in her appeals, was found guilty of recruiting and grooming young women and girls for Epstein, who died by suicide in prison in 2019 while awaiting his own trial on trafficking charges. In October, the Supreme Court declined to review whether prosecutors fairly brought a case against her.

open image in gallery Ghislaine Maxwell’s latest attempt to overturn her sex trafficking conviction and prison sentencing was rejected by a federal judge who argued her claims are ‘demonstrably meritless, and generally based on speculation, distortions, and/or outright falsehoods’ ( PA Media )

Last year, President Donald Trump reluctantly agreed to sign a measure approved by Congress that compels the Justice Department to release all investigative materials from the Epstein case in its possession.

Then-Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche also interviewed Maxwell as part of the Justice Department’s revived investigations into Epstein-related cases. Shortly after the interview last summer, Maxwell was transferred to a minimum-security women’s prison in Texas.

In December, she filed a petition for her release from prison, citing “substantial new evidence” had emerged in her case, alleging constitutional violations that she believes undermined her right to a fair trial. She argued her 2021 conviction should be rendered “invalid, unsafe and infirm,” she wrote earlier this year.

After the release of millions of documents and images in connection with investigations into Epstein and Maxwell, Maxwell argued that “further factual development is necessary.”

open image in gallery Maxwell argued that ‘further factual development is necessary’ in her case after the Justice Department’s release of the Epstein files, but those documents do not have ‘any potential to disturb the outcome of her trial,’ according a federal judge ( PA Media )

She submitted her latest request, which she wrote herself, inside a USB drive mailed in a FedEx envelope postmarked April 16, according to court documents.

But her arguments are nearly all “procedurally barred” from being put forward at this stage, after “the overwhelming testimonial and documentary evidence” at trial “conclusively established her guilt,” Judge Engelmayer wrote Tuesday.

Her petition’s claims “are demonstrably meritless, and generally based on speculation, distortions, and/or outright falsehoods,” he added.

“There is no fact that Maxwell fairly puts in dispute that has any potential to disturb the outcome of her trial,” the judge wrote.

The Independent has requested comment from Maxwell’s attorney.

Maxwell is the only convicted accomplice in the Epstein investigation to have talked to a House committee investigating the dead sex offender and an alleged network of powerful figures connected to the wealthy and well-connected financier.

She invoked her Fifth Amendment right to decline to answer any of the panel’s questions during a February deposition, and she has refused to voluntarily testify to Congress without assurances that she can receive some form of clemency. Trump and some House Republicans have not unequivocally rejected the idea of a presidential pardon, but Blanche has said he “ruled out” recommending one.

Mike Lindell, the MyPillow founder and election conspiracy theorist who lost the Republican Minnesota governor’s primary race, has missed the deadline to post funds for the recount that he demanded.

Lindell, who was endorsed by President Donald Trump, lost the gubernatorial GOP primary to Speaker of the Minnesota House, Lisa Demuth, by about 45,000 votes on August 11 and refused to concede on election night. He has since claimed “major deviations and anomalies on election night,” despite a lack of evidence.

He then launched a fundraising drive to come up with the money to cover the cost of a recount, which must take place within five days of the canvass of a primary election, per Minnesota law, asking his supporters to donate.

Despite claiming to have the $825,000 “primed and ready” to meet Monday night’s deadline, Lindell’s team said he was asking Minnesota to waive the deadline and claimed the parameters of the recount proposed by state officials were an “unlawful bait and switch.”

open image in gallery Mike Lindell, the MyPillow founder and election conspiracy theorist who lost the Republican Minnesota governor’s primary race, has missed the deadline to post funds for the recount that he demanded ( Reuters )

The campaign disputed the state’s plan for a recount on the grounds that it would only recount votes received for Lindell and Demuth, as opposed to all of the candidates.

Cassondra Knudson, spokesperson for Minnesota Secretary of State Steve Simon, said a contingent plan recount was presented to Lindell after it was approved by the State Canvassing Board on August 18. “The plan follows state law and administrative rules on recount procedures and is consistent with plans of its kind for the past two decades,” Knudson said.

Lindell’s team said the MAGA businessman was launching “immediate legal action” in response.

Minnesota Republicans previously questioned Lindell’s eligibility to run. Lindell, a Minnesota native, who stepped down as CEO of his pillow enterprise to run for governor, and had been living in Texas before he returned to the North Star State in 2025.

“I've been a resident here for a year and a half — six months early before I was required to — so he's putting out lies to get media out there,” Lindell said, referring to questions from Minnesota GOP chair Alex Plechash.

Despite launching his campaign for Minnesota governor, Lindell also was not registered to vote in the state until late July. Lindell had said he planned to register on the day he voted, which is allowed in Minnesota. But ultimately, records obtained by the Minnesota Star Tribune showed he registered earlier than Election Day.

open image in gallery Lindell, who was endorsed by President Donald Trump, lost the gubernatorial GOP primary to Speaker of the Minnesota House, Lisa Demuth, by about 45,000 votes ( AFP/Getty )

Lindell was a prominent voice in pushing the president’s false claims of widespread election fraud after he lost the 2020 election to former President Joe Biden.

His perpetuation that the election was rigged led to defamation lawsuits from Dominion Voting Systems and Smartmatic, manufacturers of voting machines. Dominion Voting Systems settled its lawsuit with Lindell, but separately, Lindell was ordered to pay $2.3 million in damages to a former Dominion employee.

In July, Trump endorsed Lindell on Truth Social, calling him “SPECTACULAR” and claiming “he deserves everything he gets.” In another July post, the president insisted Lindell would be a “GREAT” governor.

Trump even tried to give Lindell a last-minute push on election day morning by urging Minnesotans to vote for Lindell, which ultimately failed.

The president has since blamed his endorsement losses on his feeling “obligated” to go with the candidates. “It was almost impossible for them to win but, I felt obligated to go with them because they were, in my opinion, good people!” he said Sunday.

Ariana Baio contributed to this report

The United Nations and the International Committee of the Red Cross intensified a joint appeal on Tuesday for countries to enact bans and restrictions on autonomous weapons systems — often called killer robots — warning that "the risks have intensified."

Building on a proposal first issued three years ago and years of multilateral discussions, the stance stops short of requesting a complete ban.

It highlights that such systems are currently under development, though neither the U.N. nor the Red Cross has confirmed their deployment on the battlefield. Still, protections for civilians are urgently required for when that moment comes.

open image in gallery The United Nations and the International Red Cross are urging countries to adopt bans and restrictions on autonomous weapons systems, often called killer robots ( Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved. )

"We are now dangerously close to crossing a moral red line: The autonomous targeting of humans by machines," said U.N. Geneva spokesperson Alessandra Vellucci, reading a joint statement by U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres and ICRC President Mirjana Spoljaric.

"Today, we renew this call with even greater urgency," the statement declared, noting that while fundamental concerns remain the same, the underlying dangers have grown.

The two international bodies warned that military technology is evolving at "record speed," pressuring international legal frameworks and widening the gap between technical capabilities and regulation.

open image in gallery A satellite image shows smoke rising from an Ozon warehouse as Ukraine widens a campaign of drone strikes on Russian e-commerce companies, in Enem, Adygeya ( Vantor )

"Autonomous weapons systems are not part of a distant future — a race toward greater autonomy in weapons systems is already well underway," the joint statement said.

The appeal comes as negotiators prepare to convene in Geneva this November to strengthen the Convention on Conventional Weapons, a conference the U.N. and Red Cross said offers "the clearest path available" toward legally binding rules.

A yearslong campaign to limit lethal autonomous weapons systems has struggled to establish clear boundaries. The renewed push comes amid growing reliance on drones and related technologies in ongoing conflicts in Ukraine, the Middle East, Sudan, and elsewhere.

"Scientists and engineers developing these systems have themselves raised the alarm," the organizations stated. "When the architects of this technology are calling for limits, states cannot afford to remain passive."

"This year must mark a turning point," the statement added.

Marketa Vondrousova has lodged an appeal with the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) against her four-year ban for refusing an anti-doping test.

The 2023 Wimbledon champion refused an out-of-competition test at her home in December 2025 and was suspended in June by the International Tennis Integrity Agency (ITIA). A hearing date has not yet been set by the court.

Vondrousova, 27, stated in April that when she refused the test on the evening of 3 December she was at “breaking point after months of physical and mental stress”.

She claimed that the officer did not follow “protocol” and it fell outside of her allotted whereabouts slot. The Czech signed a refusal form before taking her dog for a walk.

Tennis players are required to log their whereabouts for a specific hour each day with anti-doping authorities so they can be tested outside of competition, although tests can also occur outside these set windows.

The officer who visited her in December arrived at 8.15pm, outside her whereabouts submission slot for the day, and demanded an immediate test, which Vondrousova described as a “serious intrusion into my privacy”.

But a tribunal later ruled that the Czech had “no compelling justification” for refusing the test. A test taken three days later returned negative.

In a statement following her ban, Vondrousova said: “I have never doped, I have never had a positive test. Throughout my entire career I have undergone countless anti-doping controls and have always stepped on the court with a clear conscience.”

Vondrousova was previously ranked No 6 in the world but she has not played in 2026 and has fallen to No 153. She won a silver medal at the delayed Tokyo Olympic Games and reached the final of the 2019 French Open.

Her ban is set to expire on 21 June, 2030.

News.title: The life and light of Mariam Abu Dagga  – Independent Arabia journalist killed by Israel in Gaza

Reaching into the body bag, and gently cradling her face, a family member places a mobile phone next to Mariam Abu Dagga's ear.

It is a devastating moment. Mariam, a journalist for Independent Arabia, has just been killed in an Israeli double-tap strike on the last functioning hospital in southern Gaza. She is surrounded by mourners in a tableau of grief.

On the phone is her only child, 14-year-old Ghaith. And he is saying goodbye.

He is more than 1,000 miles away, after his mother fought hard for him to be evacuated to safety in the UAE a year earlier.

And so - amid Israel's unprecedented siege and bombardment of Gaza - this is the only way for the distraught young boy to say goodbye.

“Honestly… I was against my son being away from me, because he is quite literally my life itself,” Mariam had said about Ghaith, in tears, during one of the last interviews she gave shortly before she was killed.

“But every day, I was filming the martyrs - children, just children - to the point where one day I imagined Ghaith among them.”

open image in gallery Mariam Abu Dagga with her son Ghaith ( Family handout )

Over a year had passed since he left, she explains in the interview to Palestinian organisation Filastiniyat, struggling to speak.

“He still follows the news… Whenever there were reports of journalists being targeted and I am not online, he would call me. ‘Mum, are you okay? Please tell me you're safe. Reassure me’.

“It gave me the feeling that there was someone… who truly cared about me.”

And now with his worst fears realised, this is the last phone call Ghaith will make to his mother. This time it is to say goodbye, in the hope that somewhere her soul would hear it.

Israel killed 33-year-old Mariam on 25 August 2025, while she was covering the bombing of her colleague, Reuters cameraman Hussam al-Masri. Israel had killed Hussam around eight minutes earlier, while he tended to his camera which was broadcasting the Reuters livestream from Nasser Hospital, a building protected under international law. She had rushed to the scene to find out what had happened.

This meant her killing was live-streamed to the world. A friend of Mariam's, Ghad TV correspondent Ibrahim Qannan, was filming it all from his live position just a few metres away in the aftermath of the first tank projectile which blew up Hussam.

open image in gallery Mourners, including Baraa on the left, collapse around Mariam ( Supplied )

In Ibrahim's footage, you can see Mariam there in a white headscarf and black abaya. Any journalist who covers conflict will instantly recognise that intense concentration: she is entirely focused, intently filming the rescue mission on her mobile. No time to think, to process her own grief or the enormity of the situation around her. In that moment she is her job.

As the crowd of journalists, first responders, medics and civilians grows on the stairwell, there is a second deafening boom, and Mariam is swallowed up in a fury of exploded shrapnel, concrete, wood and dust forever. Killed that day at the same hospital she was born in.

Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu dismissed the killings of around 22 people as a "tragic mishap". The Israeli military claimed the target was a camera "positioned by Hamas… to observe the activity of IDF troops" and later identified six people it called Hamas militants. Reuters soon confirmed the camera as their live feed.

A year-long investigation and reconstruction by The Independent, published today, paints a very different story to Israel’s claims, uncovering what international law experts have said is evidence of violations of international law and likely war crimes.

open image in gallery Mariam was a respected journalist who dedicated her life to covering the conflict in Gaza ( Family handout )

The Independent shared these findings with the military who declined to respond to them but added “the review is still ongoing under the General Staff Fact-Finding and Assessment Mechanism”. In the past the military has in multiple statement to The Independent repeatedly denied targeting journalists or committing any war crimes in Gaza.

Mariam was beloved by those she lived and worked alongside. That is not kindly editorialising, applied posthumously because people can't speak ill of the dead.

Her family, a dozen different journalists and people who lived and worked around Nasser were unanimous in their praise. She was a "blessing", "remarkable", "selfless", "kind", "determined", "dedicated", "a sister among us".

"She was deeply, genuinely human, not just a journalist," says Baraa Lafi, 30, her best friend, flatmate and fellow journalist, also injured in the hospital attack.

"Every story Mariam went to film, she felt the pain of people living it," the Swedish-Palestinian journalist continues, finding it hard to go back to that day.

In the footage of Mariam's body laid out on the ground, Baraa is seen kneeling next to Mariam, her head back, leaning on a wall beside her, lost in an obliterating, incomprehensible grief.

open image in gallery Mariam and Baraa working in Gaza ( Family handout )

Mariam started working as a photographer in 2016 after graduating with a degree in Journalism and Media Studies. But in her own words, she played with toy cameras as a child and pretended to take photos as if they were real.

She had covered multiple wars and crises: it was around the 2021 conflict in Gaza that she started working with Independent Arabia, alongside the Associated Press and Médecins Sans Frontières.

When Israel unleashed its heaviest ever bombardment of Gaza in the wake of Hamas militants' deadly 7 October 2023 attacks, she decided to stay and keep reporting on Israel’s retaliation, which has been so intense that a UN Commission of Enquiry has concluded it is a genocide. She kept working despite the fact that the Committee for the Protection of Journalists (CPJ) warned that Gaza was one of the most dangerous places on earth for journalists and that Israel has killed more media workers than any other nation on record. (Israel denies targeting journalists and has rejected the accusations of genocide).

She worked closely with her brother Siddiq who would accompany her, often filming her for her reports.

"Anything that happened, you'd find her there first. With her energy and drive she would be there before the event even started, no one could beat her to it, you know?" he says.

open image in gallery Mariam is one of hundreds of journalists killed in the war so far ( Family handout )

Through that Mariam was very active on social media; many posts focused on children and their inconsolable mothers going through the many stages of grief. She also added her own voice as she too lived through displacement, hunger and bombing.

"The days have become indistinguishable from one another. This is the reality we are living," she says in one reel posted to Facebook as she walks through a destroyed street.

Mariam could have found a way out of Gaza with her son but also chose to remain to support her parents.

She nursed her beloved mother, who had cancer and died in May 2024 in the middle of multiple displacements and unprecedented bombing, because there was little treatment or medicine.

In 2015 Mariam had given her kidney to her sick father Riyad Abu Dagga. In his grief, he says his one small consolation is that she quite literally "remains with me always".

Mohamed Abu Shahma, another Palestinian journalist who, like Mariam, was from Khan Younis, says one of the reasons she stayed in Gaza was to try to find her father food and water during the famine, because he needed special care and nutrition.

Mariam always put others and her work first, Baraa adds.

There were multiple times when Mariam shared her last piece of bread to stop Baraa going hungry. Once Mariam tried, at midnight and on her own, to rescue Baraa and her family when they were trapped under siege and intense bombing in the southern city of Rafah.

"She would often step away from filming to comfort the children," Baraa says.

open image in gallery The hospital stairwell seconds before the bombing ( Al Ghad/The Independent )

But such misery took its toll.

"Losing my mother was the hardest thing. My life changed completely after that, there was no life left as I knew it," Mariam says in her interview with Filastiniyat, dressed in her blue press body armour, sitting on rubble and wiping away a tear.

"Because of this war, I had to send my son to the UAE, which was also incredibly difficult.

"These were the two hardest events of my life, not just of the war, but of my entire life, because my existence was anchored to those two people: my son and my mother."

Three days before she was killed, she sent a desperate message to Hadi Torfi, assistant editor-in-chief at Independent Arabia, saying she feared she would be displaced again.

Following a well-documented pattern of Israel encircling, bombing and laying siege to large medical centres they claimed were being used by militants, there were concerns Nasser Hospital would be next.

As she speaks, it is clear she is sick: the voice note is perforated by deep, chest-wracking coughs.

"We've been told to evacuate," she says, asking Hadi if they are still tracking her for her safety.

"If I find a place in Al-Mawasi, I will let you know, because until now I don't know where to go… I have nowhere to go."

open image in gallery Mariam and her beloved mother who died from cancer in the middle of the war no Gaza ( Family handout )

But she never stopped working. Around the same time she also sent a message to Mohamad Ghandour, one of the other editors at Independent Arabia, who bonded with Mariam because, as a Lebanese citizen, his family home in south Lebanon had also been destroyed by Israel.

"She was born with a camera in her hands," he continues, adding that she struggled to juggle being a reporter, mother and victim.

Towards the end, Mariam felt "surrounded by death", her friends said. Prominent Palestinian journalist Anas al-Sharif, who worked for Al Jazeera, had been killed just a few weeks before in an Israeli targeted assassination on his tent in Al-Shifa Hospital in Gaza City.

Like so many Palestinian journalists, she wrote several wills in case the worst happened, including one for her son, in which she urged him to flourish, become a businessman and not cry if the worst happened. Her last posthumous request to her beloved boy was that, if he has a daughter, she be called Mariam.

She left these testaments with Baraa, who had the horrific task of delivering them.

Mariam had moments of feeling inconsolably bleak, and admitted more than once to wanting to "throw the camera away". She felt they were documenting a genocide in real time and the world shrugged in return.

But as always, she never gave up.

"The difficulties and the targeting we faced actually made us more attached to the profession, despite the danger and the harsh conditions we were living through," she says in her final interview - defiant in her press jacket amid the ashen rubble.

"We are continuing with our press coverage to convey the message to the outside world. We held on even tighter to this profession, our love for it grew."

*With additional reporting by Nedal Hamdouna and Ezzedine Abu Aisha in Gaza

News.title: Trump’s nutrition advisor jokes kids should eat food fresh from the ground - like hot dogs

President Donald Trump’s nutrition adviser has said kids should eat food fresh from the ground, and then jokingly suggested hot dogs as an option - as a real-life dog interrupted his address.

During an event to promote nutritious school meals from local farmers on Monday, Dr. Ben Carson talked about teaching children where their food comes from and having them taste veggies straight from the soil.

“I remember not too many months ago, [Agriculture] Secretary [Brooke] Rollins and I went to a school, and we were giving the children whole milk. They were just so amazed. They said, ‘I didn’t know milk could taste this good!’ And what if we introduced them to food fresh from the ground? Teaching them — making these relationships with the farmers so they learn about the soil. They learn about irrigation. They learn about the effect that it has on their crop,” Carson said.

Carson then listed some examples of food children could eat on these farms, with one processed meat item catching the audience’s attention.

“They get an opportunity to eat a tomato fresh off the vine. It’s a different food than you get in the store, quite frankly. Fresh sweet corn...and hot dogs,” Carson said to laughter right after a dog barked in the audience. “But what a difference it makes when they can taste these things. They won’t have a craving for the unhealthy foods that are so prevalent in our society.”

open image in gallery President Donald Trump’s nutrition adviser joked kids should eat food fresh from the ground like hot dogs ( AFP/Getty )

Carson, a former neurosurgeon and an opponent of Trump during the 2016 presidential election, was sworn in as the national advisor for nutrition, health and housing at the Department of Agriculture last September. He also served as Trump’s Department of Housing and Urban Development secretary during his first presidential term.

His comment about feeding children comes as the Trump team pushes the “Make America Healthy Again” movement, which scrutinizes ultra-processed foods.

In late July, Kennedy grossly underestimated ingredient costs while presenting a recipe on his cooking show, The Real Food Show, which is focused on healthy, affordable meals. Instead of calculating how much it costs to buy the whole ingredient, just the price of each serving of the ingredient needed for the recipe was shown.

open image in gallery Dr. Ben Carson from the Department of Agriculture listed ‘fresh sweet corn and hot dogs’ as examples of food children could eat straight from local farms at an event Monday ( Getty/iStock )

As Washington Post columnist Monica Hesse noted in an article, “that kind of practical thinking is not helpful to a parent who has $20 in cash to get them to tomorrow’s paycheck.

“Safeway does not let you walk in, scoop some mayo out of a jar and pay one dollar at the cash register. You have to buy the whole thing.”

Rollins was also roasted earlier this year for suggesting Americans eat “a piece of chicken, a piece of broccoli, corn tortilla and one other thing” as a budget meal.

“‘You should eat prison meals’ prob not the best message,” Variety’s Chief Correspondent Marlow Stern wrote on X at the time.

Carson was at the Agriculture Department’s Washington, D.C. headquarters on Monday to support Rollins and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s new “Harvest to Hallways” initiative as part of the administration’s MAHA agenda.

open image in gallery The Washington, DC, event Carson attended was promoting a new initiative part of the ‘Make America Healthy Again’ movement, which scrutinizes ultra-processed foods ( Getty )

The initiative will include a $50 million investment in school cafeterias, which, in part, will help pay for new equipment and up to $25 million in grants for schools to provide kids with locally grown foods.

These investments in healthy school lunches come at a time when a packed lunch for children costs more than $6, and Americans struggle to pay for their grocery bills.

While many school districts do offer some kind of cafeteria lunch for free, or at a reduced price, fewer children automatically qualify due to changes to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program made under the Trump administration.

This article was amended the day after publication. It previously reported Carson’s hot dog comments without noting they were intended as a joke.

News.title: Palmer and Rogers show promise of star double act for Chelsea
News.content:
“I am very happy for Cole,” Alonso said. “I have really enjoyed seeing him play with the dynamism and the freedom and the responsibility... when Cole feels this way we have a better team and a better Cole.”

Palmer makes it look very easy in this form, capable of switching the direction of play a beat before anyone else spots the opportunity. He and his old Manchester City academy friend Rogers came off before the end, Palmer having demonstrated some discomfort chasing a ball. Asked afterwards how ready he felt, Palmer responded in kind. “Did you not watch the game? I’m only joking, I’m ready... it was a difficult season with injuries and whatnot, but through the summer and since I’ve been back I’ve worked extra hard.”

If there was an attacker to compare with him on the other side it was King, who looks even better. The 19-year-old was way ahead of Arbeloa’s two young Real Madrid imports. García toiled away and took his chance, but César Palacios struggled for any impact in a position tucked in on the left. Oscar Bobb and King gave Fulham some edge but the concern, as ever, will be where Fulham get their goals.

Arbeloa pushed his full-backs high and encouraged Sander Berge to drop deep to get on the ball in the first passing phase. The Norwegian delayed too long in challenging João Pedro for Chelsea’s third – backing off and allowing Palmer to overlap to receive the pass.

Sánchez had not been the only concern for Chelsea. Back in the team, Levi Colwill misjudged a challenge on King in the first half and was relieved that the card was only yellow. Roméo Lavia took a wild swing at Calvin Bassey and was also booked. Moisés Caicedo was not fit to play. Enzo Fernández was on the bench and would come on in the second half to the kind of reception from opposition fans to which he will quickly become familiar.

There was a grin from the Argentine at those who berated him from the home stands when he returned at half-time. Fernández worked hard to transmit a general sense that the abuse did not land, although he will be relieved that the Chelsea fans were supportive. His future still feels very much in play.

It was Palmer’s subtle ball through that gave João Pedro the chance with 32 seconds of the game played. The ball came forward immediately from Lacroix’s firm header from defence. The Frenchman delivered a very accomplished assist for Rogers’s first-half goal. Before that King had equalised. There was an exchange with Timothy Castagne, and King looked up just inside the box and decided to have a swing at it. Sánchez was close enough to grasp the ball and somehow failed to do so.

Sánchez would later push a Castagne shot in the direction of García, who stooped and nodded the ball over the goalkeeper after Palmer had scored Chelsea’s third. This second error was unfortunate, but it is the kind of thing that happens to a goalkeeper as erratic as the one for whom Chelsea’s hierarchy seem to have such patience.
