World.title: Greece seeks to cash in on Odyssey ‘hype’
World.content:
Perhaps most crucially for the Greek economy, officials are now seeking to translate that renewed interest in the Cyclops and man-eating Laestrygonians into tourist revenue.

The Greek National Tourism Organization organized a press trip to Odysseus’ home island of Ithaca — to which he struggled to return after the Trojan War — that resulted in a 162-page publication by Le Figaro magazine, titled “In the Footsteps of Odysseus.”

The Peloponnese region is creating a thematic travel program, called “The Odyssey Route — Homer’s Peloponnese,” which will likely be ready by November. The regional authorities are currently designing the signs and website that will guide tourists.

“The aim is to link Homer’s epics and the film production, connect the production locations with other locations in the Peloponnese, associated with the myth itself,” said the deputy regional governor for tourism in the Peloponnese region, Thanasis Michelongonas.

Such locations include the islet of Cranae, where, according to legend, Paris of Troy took Helen for their first night after abducting her from Sparta. Or the tiny islet of Pefnos, where Zeus took refuge in the form of a swan and seduced (or assaulted) Leda, who subsequently gave birth to the famous egg from which Helen of Troy hatched.

“We want to capitalize on the hype created,” Michelongonas said. “Expectations are probably greater than reality. Of course, that doesn’t change the fact that we’ve received a great deal of publicity, worth millions and it’s up to us to make the most of it.”

World.title: Trump slams Tehran for executing protesters at levels 'not seen before'
World.content:
US President Donald Trump has renewed his criticism of Iran's execution of protesters, claiming Tehran can no longer afford to fund its armed forces and is facing a humanitarian crisis "of epic proportions".

 

"The failing Islamic Republic of Iran is not paying large segments of their military, while at the same time killing protesters, even when they are not protesting, at levels not seen before," Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform on Tuesday.

"It is a humanitarian crisis of epic proportions, and must be stopped, now," he added.

In January, warning of imminent executions, Trump said the United States would take "very severe action" if they went ahead.

Days later he said reliable sources had informed him that the executions of "more than 800 detained protesters" had been halted, a claim Iranian officials did not confirm.

In April, Trump said eight Iranian women shown in a photograph circulating online had been sentenced to death and called for their release. The following day he said they had been pardoned.

A Euronews Persian investigation, citing two independent human rights organisations, found that only one of the eight women, Beita Hemmati, had actually received a death sentence.

Last month Trump reposted material about the execution of protesters and, reacting to the killing of Gol-Mohammad Mohammadi, a 23-year-old demonstrator, called the Islamic Republic "barbaric".

Iran's escalating execution rate

International concern over Tehran's use of the death penalty against protesters has grown significantly.

On 12 August, 32 countries including France, the UK and Canada issued a joint statement condemning the Islamic Republic's use of capital punishment to "silence dissent" and calling for an immediate halt to executions and the release of those arbitrarily detained.

UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk said Tehran was using executions to "create fear".

"Since 19 March 2026 at least 56 people have been executed on charges related to national security, including 27 in cases linked to the January protests," Türk said in a statement this month, adding that more than 100 others were at risk of execution.

The Abdorrahman Boroumand Centre, an Iranian human rights organisation based in Washington, recorded at least 901 executions in Iran in the first seven months of 2026, 56 of them on political or national security charges. Of those, at least 29 were executed in connection with the January protests.

The January 2026 protests erupted following the collapse of the Iranian rial the month before and spread rapidly to more than 180 cities.

Security forces killed thousands of people during a crackdown on 8 and 9 January in the resulting crackdown.

Iran's Supreme Council of National Security acknowledged a death toll of more than 3,000. The UN Special Rapporteur on Iran put the figure at at least 5,000, while human rights groups and insiders in Iran believe the actual number of those killed may have surpassed 32,000.

At least 1,639 people were executed in Iran in 2025, the highest annual figure since 1989, according to Iran Human Rights and the organisation Together Against the Death Penalty.

World.title: Spain to reform asylum laws to align with EU rules as Ceuta crisis remains unresolved
World.content:
The Spanish government is expected to present a draft bill to reform immigration and asylum laws as it struggles to contain the political fallout of the Ceuta crisis, which saw 80,000 people cross illegally from Morocco into the Spanish city in one day in July.

 

Madrid said the aim is to “bring Spanish legislation into line with the European Pact on Migration and Asylum”, which came into force this summer. However, the timing comes as the migrant crisis in Ceuta remains unresolved.

While the vast majority of the 80,000 people who crossed the border illegally have returned to Morocco, around 5,000 remain in the Spanish enclave, including an estimated 2,000 minors.

The issue of unaccompanied minors is particularly sensitive, as Madrid seeks to balance strict legal requirements with its commitments to Brussels and Ceuta’s regional authorities to return everyone who entered illegally.

An attempt to transfer the minors to mainland Spain through an emergency decree has stalled, as the Spanish government, the conservative opposition and Ceuta’s regional authorities remain divided over the procedure.

Meanwhile, the European Commission has said Spain must carry out returns where there are no legal grounds for a person to remain in EU territory, while also ensuring that the rights of minors are protected under international conventions.

Madrid has yet to find a solution.

The draft immigration and asylum bill approved on Tuesday goes beyond Ceuta. It will implement the broader European Pact on Migration and Asylum, which came into force on 12 June, and introduce the EU's so-called “screening” procedure. The legislation will also affect the Canary Islands, which have seen an increase in irregular arrivals by boat.

A single command to deal with an unresolved crisis

The Spanish government also declared the Ceuta crisis a matter “of interest to national security” and called for a single command to manage the response.

The decision came almost a month after the crisis began, prompting sharp criticism from the conservative opposition People's Party (PP). Juan Vivas, president of Ceuta, had spent weeks calling on the Spanish government to take control of a situation that had overwhelmed the autonomous city.

Spain has yet to provide a comprehensive explanation of what triggered the mass influx into Ceuta, beyond pointing to human traffickers and a social media campaign that allegedly led young Moroccans and sub-Saharan migrants to believe they could enter the city and automatically claim asylum

While several ministers have been dispatched to the city, Pedro Sánchez is yet to address the migrant crisis in public since visiting Ceuta on July 31, when he declared that Spain’s territorial integrity “had been breached”, without blaming Morocco for the influx.

Rabat has said Madrid’s mass regularisation of migrants earlier this year sent contradictory signals.

World.title: Euronews exclusive: EU officials to travel to China as October deadline for trade rebalancing looms
World.content:
A group of EU officials will travel to China in the coming days to advance trade talks, as Brussels seeks to narrow a record €1 billion-a-day trade deficit with Beijing, Euronews has learned.

 

The European Commission hopes the technical discussions will deliver “tangible” results by October, when EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič is expected to travel to China.

However, talks launched by the Commission and Beijing in June have become strained in recent weeks after China barred companies from providing information to Brussels in investigations under the Foreign Subsidies Regulation, the EU's rules aimed at preventing unfair subsidies from abroad.

“No organisation or individual may execute or assist in the execution of such improper extraterritorial jurisdiction measures,” China's Ministry of Justice said in a statement on 19 August, referring to the EU's ongoing investigation into Chinese e-commerce giant JD.com following its €2.5 billion bid for German electronics retailer Ceconomy.

The probe comes as an OECD report found earlier this year that China's subsidies to companies were up to eight times higher than those provided by OECD members. The EU is also facing a surge in cheap Chinese imports, putting growing pressure on European industry.

Brussels did not stop its investigations

Despite the current sensitive talks, Brussels did not stop its investigations into what it sees as unfair trade practices coming from China, opening several anti-dumping cases over the summer.

The Commission is under pressure from EU member states, which gave President Ursula von der Leyen a mandate at a summit last June to review the bloc's trade defence tools and pursue a dialogue with Beijing aimed at delivering concrete results.

The first step came a few weeks later, when Šefčovič met his Chinese counterpart, Wang Wentao, in Brussels for political talks that formally opened negotiations between the EU and China.

The two sides agreed to establish a joint monitoring mechanism to exchange data and track trade flows “with a view to improving transparency, enhancing mutual trust and managing trade frictions”, according to a statement.

Market access is high on the agenda. China accuses the EU of shutting its market to Chinese companies through new regulations, while EU member states are seeking greater access to China for European businesses.

Brussels also chose October as a deadline for a reason: it will mark the end of a one-year truce over China's exports of rare earths, following Beijing's decision to halt all exports during its trade war with the US.

For the EU, securing continued access to these critical minerals is crucial, as they are essential to the bloc's green technology, automotive and defence industries.

World.title: What to know as Greenland presents its forced contraception reports this week
World.content:
Greenland will present two long-awaited reports on Friday 28 August examining human rights violations linked to historic cases in which Greenlandic women and girls were subjected to the insertion of intrauterine devices (IUDs) and other forms of contraception, including whether Denmark’s actions could meet the legal definition of genocide.

 

An intrauterine device (IUD) is a form of contraception placed in the uterus to prevent pregnancy. More than 4,000 Greenlandic women and girls had IUDs inserted during a Danish-led contraception campaign that began in the 1960s, with many later saying they had not been properly informed or had not consented.

The findings will arrive just one day after the Danish parliament is due to finalise compensation legislation for affected women, raising questions about how the reports’ assessment of responsibility will sit alongside Denmark’s existing response.

Denmark ran Greenland's health care system until 1992. In 2024, the Greenlandic self-government asked independent experts to investigate whether the Danish state committed a genocide and violated international law.

"As a society, we must have all the facts on the table, but we must also find ways to move forward together. Therefore, the investigation will also address how the trauma caused by the Contraception Case has affected society over generations,” the Greenlandic government wrote in a statement in 2024.

The results are now due to be published on Friday.

The new investigation is separate from a previous joint Danish-Greenlandic historical report published in September 2025, which was followed by a public apology from Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen. While that investigation reconstructed what happened and how the contraception programme was carried out, the new reports examine how those practices should be understood under human rights and international law.

What the reports will cover

The reports being published on Friday will not themselves establish legally binding responsibility, according to legal experts.

“[There will be] no strict legal effect from the reports. However, depending on the results, they might lead to political action,” Sune Klinge, an associate professor specialising in constitutional law at the University of Copenhagen, told Euronews Health.

Some experts say the case is unlikely to meet the legal threshold for genocide.

“The [United Nations] Genocide Convention coupled with judicial practice will be the legal basis for a finding of responsibility for genocide. Genocide is based on the perpetrator’s special intent to commit the acts because he or she does not recognise the group’s right to exist as a group,” Frederik Harhoff, an international law scholar at the University of Southern Denmark and former judge at the United Nations International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, told Euronews Health.

“It is therefore unlikely that the report will conclude that genocide took place, and if one of the two reports does so, they are wrong,” Harhoff added.

He also said that while a public report may be indicative, criminal responsibility for genocide can only be established by a competent court.

The reports could also identify other violations of international human rights or indigenous peoples’ rights, which could still shape the political and legal response to the case.

Their significance may therefore lie partly in what governments, affected women and courts choose to do with the findings afterwards.

“As genocide cannot be established for lack of the required special intent, violation of the women’s human rights becomes essential,” Harhoff added.

Why are there two reports?

Greenland originally appointed one four-person expert group to carry out the human rights investigation.

However, the group later split into two over what the government has described as “disagreements on the professional approach”, leaving Greenland ultimately receiving two reports rather than one.

The Greenlandic government said both reports subsequently underwent external review of their methodology and academic standards.

It has not disclosed whether the disagreement extended to the experts’ conclusions or who authored each of the two reports.

Related Greenland women seek urgent compensation for forced contraception

Expert urged the reports to be published sooner

The timing of the publication has already attracted criticism because Denmark is moving ahead with its compensation legislation before the assessments are made public.

The reports were already completed and handed to Greenland’s government in February, but their publication was delayed while they were translated, peer-reviewed and prepared for public release.

The Danish parliament is due to hold the compensation bill’s final vote on Thursday, one day before the Greenlandic government presents the reports.

Under the proposed scheme, eligible women subjected to contraception without consent during the period when Denmark was responsible for Greenland’s healthcare would be entitled to DKK 300,000 (€40,000).

Earlier this month, one of the experts commissioned to investigate the case, Jonas Christoffersen, urged Greenland’s government to publish the reports before the Danish parliament completed its compensation legislation, arguing that lawmakers should have access to the findings before adopting the law.

"It is fundamentally questionable in a democracy that the [Danish parliament] will pass a law without knowing about the reports that independent individuals have written. The Greenland Government should therefore immediately publish the reports, just as the [Danish parliament] should be made aware of them, so that the entire matter can be debated on a fully informed basis,” Christoffersen wrote in a statement.

“The case has damaged the relationship between Denmark and Greenland, and in my opinion it is best for everyone if there is full transparency about the matter," he added.

Harhoff also regards the parliament’s decision to proceed with the bill without waiting for the reports as a ”mistake”.

However, he said the compensation scheme would not prevent Greenlandic women from pursuing further legal action if the reports identify broader human rights violations or responsibility on Denmark’s part.

Klinge also said Danish politicians are “always free to amend laws and expand the scheme”, while noting that DKK 300,000 is already at the upper end of compensation awarded in comparable cases.

Earlier this month, Denmark’s health minister Ida Auken said the government did not want to wait for the reports before parliament adopted a compensation scheme for Greenlandic women affected by the contraception case.

“For us, it has been absolutely crucial that we do not delay anything. The women have waited long enough,” Auken told the local news agency, Ritzau.

World.title: Qatar says officials working daily to revive US-Iran talks, urges Tehran to reopen Hormuz
World.content:
Qatar and Pakistan are continuing efforts to revive negotiations between the US and Iran, with officials speaking to the parties daily to explore possible ways forward, Qatar’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson said on Tuesday.

 

“Our officials are on the phone on a daily basis trying to workshop ideas, workshop ways of getting back to the negotiations,” Majed Al-Ansari told reporters in Doha.

Al-Ansari did not provide details of the proposals being discussed but said Qatar remained focused on reaching a diplomatic solution to the ongoing war between the two sides.

“Our priority was always reaching a diplomatic solution through talks,” he said. “We are urging the parties to engage fully in the talks and the mediation that is led by Qatar and Pakistan and the other regional players.”

He further described negotiations as “the only way out of this crisis” and urged both sides to engage in good faith.

Qatar and Pakistan have acted as the two main mediators between the US and Iran since the outbreak of the war in late February.

Al-Ansari's comments came after Pakistan’s army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir visited Tehran for talks with senior Iranian officials as part of efforts to reduce regional tensions and revive negotiations.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian meets Pakistan's army chief Asim Munir in Tehran on 24 August 2026. (Iranian Presidency Office) AP Photo

The visit coincided with an expansion of US sanctions against Iran, which Washington has dubbed "Operation Economic Outcast".

Tehran has vowed to resist the measures, while Pakistan’s Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi said the talks in the Iranian capital had made “significant progress”.

Asked whether the new sanctions could support efforts to resolve the war, Al-Ansari said they were unilateral rather than UN or multilateral measures and that questions about their purpose should be directed to the countries imposing them.

Qatar calls for immediate reopening of Hormuz

Al-Ansari also rejected the possibility of Qatar pursuing a separate agreement with Iran to secure passage for its energy exports through Hormuz.

“This is a regional problem that needs a regional solution. It cannot be addressed bilaterally with Iran,” he said.

“Iran has closed the Strait of Hormuz in a way that goes beyond international maritime law and goes beyond good-neighbourly relations. This needs to end immediately.”

He said Doha wanted freedom of navigation restored to the conditions that existed before the war began.

The strait is a vital route for global energy supplies and is particularly important to Qatar, one of the world’s largest exporters of liquefied natural gas. Disruption to shipping through the waterway has delayed energy deliveries and raised concerns about global supplies.

Al-Ansari said other countries were entitled to negotiate their own arrangements with Iran but maintained that Qatar favoured regional talks over separate safe-passage agreements.

“For us in Qatar, we believe in regional dialogue over this,” he said. “The imperative is to go back to freedom of navigation and to the opening of the Strait of Hormuz as it was before the war.”

World.title: Trump considering renaming Lake Ontario to 'Lake America' as trade war with Canada escalates
World.content:
President Donald Trump said on Tuesday that he is considering changing the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America” as the trade war between the United States and Canada intensifies.

 

Such a change would be reminiscent of the Republican president’s unilateral action last year by executive order to rename the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America.

The United States and Canada are locked in a trade dispute, with Canada expected to announce retaliatory measures on Tuesday.

That’s in response to the Trump administration enacting 50% tariffs on $20 billion (€17 billion) of Canadian goods over the weekend after talks between the countries broke down.

“The United States is giving serious consideration to changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America in that we don’t expect to doing much business with Ontario any longer,” Trump said in a post on social media.

Ontario is Canada’s most populous province and is home to the country’s auto industry.

A screenshot of a post on US President Donald Trump's Truth Social account, 25 August, 2026 @realDonaldTrump

The rhetoric between the two countries is escalating, with Trump telling Canadian leaders on Monday to “fall in line” or face consequences “far WORSE” than existing tariffs.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has accused Washington of trying to subordinate Canada.

Trump also threatened new 50% tariffs on Canadian vehicles, auto parts and steel, while Carney said US trade demands showed that Washington wanted to “destroy our major industries,” including autos, steel and aluminium.

Canada and the United States share one of the world’s largest trading relationships, with deeply integrated supply chains across cars, energy, agriculture and manufacturing, making a prolonged trade fight potentially costly for businesses and workers on both sides of the border.

Businesses and consumers are caught in the middle, facing uncertainty about how much prices may increase.

Michael Howard II, owner of a furniture business in Warren, Michigan, outside Detroit, said the tariffs will hamper the “ability for us to put food on the table for our family, but also impacts the ability for us to give back to our community.”

Canada’s Prime Minister Mark Carney speaks in Ottawa, 22 August, 2026 The Canadian Press

Howard and his wife started their business a decade ago. They make and sell everything from dining room tables to bookcases.

“To say that we don’t need Canada is just disingenuous,” he said. “It’s dishonest. And it’s just absolutely not truthful. We need our neighbour, but also they need us.”

Canada’s Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne and three other Cabinet ministers are also expected to share details of support for workers affected by tariffs.

Carney said earlier on Monday that Canada may need to move away from matching US tariffs dollar for dollar and instead use more targeted retaliation aimed at protecting Canadian workers and businesses.

“An attitude at the negotiation table that Canada is a subsidiary of the United States” is “not something we’re going to accept,” Carney said.

Carney was even more blunt in French.

“We learned during the negotiations that the Americans want to destroy our major industries, including autos, steel and aluminium,” Carney said. “That was one of the main reasons we said no. It was a bad deal.”

World.title: Ceuta migration sparks nearly 9,600 hate posts on social media
World.content:
The latest incident in Ceuta sent hate speech on social media soaring, with 9,590 posts detected by the Spanish Observatory on Racism and Xenophobia (OBERAXE) in just two days, coinciding with the mass arrival of migrants on 30 and 31 July, which the government put at around 80,000 people.

 

The Ministry of Inclusion, Social Security and Migration says this spike pushed the number of hate-content items recorded in July to 57,406, up from 40,800 in June.

The monthly report notes that people from North Africa remain the main target of hate speech on social media, accounting for 68% of the content detected in July. Messages targeting immigrants made up 19% of the total, followed by those directed at Muslims (16%), people of African descent (10%) and Latin Americans (7%).

Public safety fears and the World Cup drove hate speech in July

Public safety was the main focus of hate speech in July, accounting for 48% of the content analysed, much of it broadly linking migration with crime.

Sport accounted for another 34% of the posts, in a context shaped by the Football World Cup, which fuelled racist, xenophobic and Islamophobic content targeting players, national teams and fans. Migration policies were the focus of 17% of the content, followed by posts about sexual assaults (5%), terrorism (4%) and the arrival of boats (1%).

OBERAXE, which reports to the State Secretariat for Migration, notes that four in ten posts dehumanise or seriously degrade the groups targeted. Some 38% contain threats, while 15% call for their expulsion and 4% incite violence. A further 2% seek to discredit them and 1% praise those who attack them.

Platforms improve removal of hate content

The report says that 60% of the content used openly aggressive language, with insults, threats and slurs. Some 34% relied on irony or sarcasm, while 33% used images, videos, memes or coded language, tools that facilitate its spread and make automatic detection harder.

The OBERAXE report highlights an improvement in platforms' removal of hate content, with platforms deleting 12% of user-reported posts, up from 10% in June.

Some 9% was taken down within the first 24 hours, while another 3% disappeared over the following week. The role of the "trusted flagger", which literally means 'trusted reporter', enabled the removal of 58% of reported content, seven points higher than the previous month.

By platform, X led takedowns with 93%, followed by TikTok (88%), Facebook (74%) and Instagram (71%). YouTube lagged well behind at 14%, although Instagram stood out by more than doubling its removal rate compared with June.

World.title: Meet the new James Bond villain? Saoirse Ronan is 'dead serious' about wanting to play a 007 baddie
World.content:
Irish actress Saoirse Ronan has doubled down on her wish to join the cast of the next James Bond film, and wants to play the next villain.

 

While the next actor to play 007 has not been revealed – even though we can expect some news on that front soon – the star of The Grand Budapest Hotel, Lady Bird, Brooklyn and Little Women says she wants to get in touch with her dark side.

“I want to go dark,” she said in a recent interview with Empire. “I said that I wanted to be a Bond villain and I’m dead serious.”

The Oscar-nominated actress continued: “I think it would be really interesting, having a young female villain. Especially for girls and women, to see someone who can just take all that pent-up anger and direct it somewhere, there’s something interesting in that dramatically. So I would love to do more of that.”

This is not the first time that Ronan has expressed her desire to play a Bond villain.

In 2024, she told Vanity Fair: “I will stand by really wanting to play a Bond villain, which I will say again and again. Because anytime that I’ve gotten a chance to play someone who’s a little bit evil, I just love it. And I think it would be really fun to do that again.”

Ronan's husband, Slow Horses star Jack Lowden, is currently considered one of the frontrunners to play 007.

Should both actors be cast in Bond 26, they would become the first married couple to star opposite one another in a James Bond movie.

Take a look at this absurdly good looking and talented pair:

Jack Lowden and Saoirse Ronan AP Photo

Make it happen, Bond casting director Nina Gold.

Oh, and while we’re at it, find yourself a partner who looks at you like this:

Saoirse Ronan and Jack Lowden AP Photo

In another 2024 interview with the Happy Sad Confused podcast, Ronan revealed that should she be faced with the ultimate choice, she would rather her husband be Bond than her being cast as a Bond villain.

Check out the footage below:

About Ronan’s campaign to become a Bond villain, we previously wrote: “Ronan would be the perfect foil for a new Bond – not just because she has the range to play any role but because she would inject an intriguing level of humanity within a level of sadism and maliciousness that we haven’t seen her fully embrace yet. More than that, if a necessary 007 renaissance is to take place for the 26th film, so should the role of the female villain.”

We added: “Traditionally, male antagonists have been the standard for the 007 franchise, and when actresses have been cast as baddies, they’ve been relegated to side-villains / secondary scoundrels. (...) It’s time the Bond series had a properly vicious primary female villain, and casting an actress of Ronan’s versatility and charisma could not only break the antiquated trend, but also take the franchise in a bold new direction.”

The search for the next James Bond is underway, with auditions reportedly taking place this month.

Reports have continued to swirl around who might next wield the Walter PPK, with Lowden, Callum Turner, Jacob Elordi, Louis Partridge and Tom Francis all rumoured frontrunners for the role.

Bond 26 will be directed by Canadian filmmaker and four-time Oscar nominee Denis Villeneuve and is being written by Peaky Blinders creator Steven Knight. Production is expected to kick off in 2027, with a release planned for 2028.

Saoirse Ronan will next be seen in Sam Mendes’ Beatles biopics as Linda McCartney, as well as Alice Rohrwacher’s highly anticipated Three Incestuous Sisters with Josh O’Connor, Dakota Johnson, Jessie Buckley (our April Fool’s pick for the next Bond) and Mick Jagger. No release date has yet been announced.

World.title: Germans swap friends for screens in their free time
World.content:
People are spending less time going out with friends and more of their leisure time online. AI is now part of that shift.

Germans are spending less of their free time socializing with friends and more on individually planned and digital activities, according to a survey published on Tuesday .

Meeting friends remains the most important social leisure activity, but its role has weakened significantly over time.

How Germans are spending their free time now

The Hamburg Foundation for Future Studies found that just 19% of 3,000 respondents said they regularly went out with friends, down from 37% when its first "Leisure Monitor" was conducted 40 years ago.

"Traditional sociability is losing reach, while social contacts are increasingly shifting toward individually planned and digital forms," said Ulrich Reinhardt, the foundation's scientific director.

He said everyday leisure was increasingly dominated by internet use, television, music and smartphones. Digital activities have grown sharply:

82% listen to music digitally at least weekly, up from 52% in 2016.

71% use social media weekly, up from 48%.

33% play video games weekly, up from 9%.

Artificial intelligence is now used at least once a week by 42% of respondents, rising to 62% among 18- to 24-year-olds.

How deep can a relationship with AI get? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Reinhardt said younger users were turning to AI not just for information, but also for advice, reassurance and, in some cases, as a substitute for friendship.

Are Germans becoming less active?

Surprisingly, the survey found that Germans were more physically active than they once were.

The survey found that 53% now exercise at least once a week, compared with just 18% in 1986.

Doing nothing or simply relaxing has also become more common, rising 15 percentage points since 2016 to 62%.

The popularity of joining clubs has remained stable, with 18% taking part weekly in sports, singing or other associations. Regular volunteering has even increased, from 6% 40 years ago to 12% today.

World.title: Nigeria's jet fuel conundrum: Scarcity at home, abundance abroad
World.content:
Nigeria is fast becoming Europe's biggest jet fuel supplier, as it continues to help ease ongoing shortages abroad. Meanwhile at home, the West African country’s own airlines are struggling to keep their tanks full.

For the past two months. Nigeria has emerged as Europe's largest supplier of jet fuel, overtaking the United States.

The 650,000 barrel-per-day (bpd) mega refinery owned by Africa's richest man, Aliko Dangote, outside Lagos has evolved into an increasingly important source of fuel for the continent following supply disruptions caused by the Iran war.

During last year's peak summer months, the majority of these supplies still originated from the Middle East.

But since the closure of the Strait of Hormuz earlier this year, Europe has been relying on imports of roughly 700,000 bpd in total to meet the present demands of the aviation industry, according to the private, global trade intelligence business Kpler.

Dry fuel tanks in Europe

In fact, back in April, the head of the International Energy Agency Fatih Birol expressed concern that at the time Europe only had "maybe six weeks or so" of jet fuel supplies remaining.

Less than two months later, four airports in northern Italy — Bologna, Venice, Treviso and Milan's Linate — even introduced temporary restrictions on jet fuel use, imposing a ceiling of 2,000 liters per aircraft for short-haul journeys, according to local media, while giving priority to medical and long-haul flights.

Europe has, in the meantime, been able to absorb the shock of the closure of the Strait of Hormuz by diversifying its resources and boosting supplies from countries like Nigeria — but at what cost?

Africa's fuel crisis: Is Dangote the answer? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Paradox of surplus production

Nigeria continues to produce a record amount of jet fuel through the Dangote refinery, equivalent to about 24 million liters each day, with much of this now being shipped to Europe.

But domestic airlines in the West African country meanwhile appear to struggle to keep up with their daily estimated needs because of the surge in prices and the demands of the free market.

Ikemesit Effiong, a partner at the Africa-focused SBM intelligence consultancy, explained that "Nigeria operates a fully deregulated downstream market where Dangote prices its products with reference to international parity, not preferential domestic rates."

"Fuel flows to wherever pays the most," he told DW, adding that "currently, that is Europe, not Lagos."

"The key lesson Nigerian players are learning is that production capacity alone does not guarantee affordability at home."

While the Dangote refinery has significantly improved fuel availability in the country, which has long been plagued by chronic fuel scarcity and long queues at petrol stations, domestic prices are still among the highest on the continent.

Passengers in Nigeria are likely to think twice before purchasing flights, as prices have skyrocketed Image: Benson Ibeabuchi/AFP/Getty Images

Local airlines struggle to keep up

In the fully deregulated Nigerian market, regional airlines also have to compete with international buyers, who typically place orders for greater purchasing volumes, often without any middlemen involved between them at the refineries; according to Effiong, this alone leave global players with significant negotiating advantages compared to smaller local companies.

"The result is that [while] domestic airlines might be physically closer to the refinery, they're economically less competitive in accessing its products. They might as well be halfway across the world," he added.

Since the beginning of the crisis, local aviation operators have reportedly accrued over 60bn Naira ($45 million; €38 million) in debt to local banks to be able to sustain operations and keep afloat during this surge in prices.

Many operators have even been forced to cut key routes and hike up ticket prices, resulting in frustration and discontent among passengers; furthermore, ongoing flight cancellations and delays only keep adding to the overall sense of dissatisfaction among travelers.

At one point, jet fuel prices jumped up over threefold soon after the start of the Iran war; they have since fallen to a minimum about 1,600 Naira per liter — which compares to roughly 900 Naira prior to the war.

Hidden costs and mark-ups

The current situation is further exacerbated by the abolition of government subsidies for oil products, as well as by Nigeria's state oil company's crude-backed loans.

This means that part of the country's future crude production to is allocated to repaying debts, leaving the Dangote Refinery to have to import its crude to refine — rather than making use of Nigeria's own reserves.

Why Nigeria's largest refinery is importing US oil To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

But the problem isn't solely focused on the source of the jet fuel itself. Charles Victor, an energy analyst based in Lagos, explained that "[t]he journey from the refinery gate to the airport is expensive with extra layers of additional cost. [These issues include] storage, coastal shipping, moving fuel between tanks, with several traders in between — and each one takes a cut."

Victor went as far as saying that "the problem was never a supply issue. It's what happens to the price on the way to the aircraft."

No solutions without government intervention?

For Victor, the solution is to reserve a certain metric ton amount of fuel for Nigerian airlines each month, and selling this directly and equitably to all stakeholders as a group.

Buying "directly from the refinery gate, if possible, will cut out most of the middlemen adding cost along the way," he told DW, saying that wholesale price could thus at least stabilize around 1,200 Naira pet liter this way.

This plan would also require improved airport storage and distribution infrastructures to "reduce logistics costs that add significantly to the final prices," Ikemesit added. "Finally, the government should institute policies that encourage sustainable commercial relationships between Dangote and domestic carriers."

But would Dangote play along with that? The Dangote Refinery, operating at its maximum capacity of 650,000 bpd, was originally built with the intention of transforming the continent's biggest oil producer into a net exporter of refined products, and thus to end its dependence on fuel imports.

However, with a global crisis situation firmly putting Dangote on the map as a worldwide supplier, that plan might remain a pipe dream.

Edited by: Sertan Sanderson

World.title: Will Iran withdraw from nuclear non-proliferation treaty?
World.content:
Iranian lawmakers have again raised the possibility of leaving a decades-old international nuclear weapons treaty. Analysts say the threat to quit may offer Tehran more leverage than an actual withdrawal.

Lawmakers in Iran have once again raised the possibility of leaving the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) as tensions over Tehran's nuclear program and its standoff with the United States continue.

Iranian MP Ghasem Ravanbakhsh said a proposal to withdraw from the landmark treaty had been submitted and was being considered.

Ebrahim Rezaei, a member of the National Security and Foreign Policy Commission, said a withdrawal would be the "best response" to increased US economic pressure.

The idea is not new. Iranian officials and lawmakers have repeatedly raised it during periods of tension with Western governments. However, it remains unclear whether Tehran is actually preparing to leave the treaty or whether the threat itself is the objective.

What would leaving the nuclear treaty mean?

In 1970, Iran ratified the agreement, which is the main international treaty on nuclear non-proliferation.

Iran has been repeatedly accused of having hidden its nuclear program Image: Planet Labs PBC/AP/picture alliance

The NPT has 191 member states and is based on preventing the spread of nuclear weapons, promoting peaceful nuclear cooperation and pursuing nuclear disarmament.

Any member can withdraw if it believes that extraordinary events related to the treaty have put its supreme national interests at risk.

It must give three months' notice to the other members and the UN Security Council and explain its reasons. Leaving the treaty is therefore legally possible.

Behrooz Bayat, a nuclear expert and former consultant to the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), told DW that the process would take time.

"A withdrawal would almost certainly be seen internationally as a signal that Iran intends either to keep open the option of developing nuclear weapons or to move toward doing so," Bayat said.

He said such a perception could sharply increase political and economic pressure and potentially raise the risk of further military action.

For that reason, Bayat believes Tehran's repeated threats are more useful as diplomatic leverage than as a policy it actually intends to pursue.

Why withdrawal may not benefit Tehran

Shahin Modarres, an international security analyst and researcher at LUISS University in Rome, told DW that the renewed debate should be seen in the context of stalled negotiations over uranium enrichment and Iran's stockpile of highly enriched uranium.

Iran has about 440 kilograms (972 pounds) of uranium that is enriched up to 60% purity, a short, technical step from weapons-grade levels of 90%, according to the IAEA.

Inspectors from the UN's nuclear watchdog were unable to verify the location of much of the material after the June 2025 US and Israeli strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities.

Iran has already sharply reduced international oversight. In July 2025, Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian signed legislation to suspend access for IAEA inspectors into the country until the "security" of its nuclear facilities is guaranteed.

That created what Modarres describes as a potentially more useful position for Tehran than formally withdrawing from the treaty.

"Withdrawal would remove that ambiguity without offering any clear advantage, turning a dispute over compliance into an explicit declaration of intent," the analyst said.

"By remaining formally within the NPT while limiting inspections, Iran can maintain uncertainty about its capabilities and intentions without openly leaving the global non-proliferation system," he added. "Withdrawing would remove much of that uncertainty."

A countdown could increase military risk

Withdrawal could also have security implications for Tehran. Under Article X of the treaty, states must give three months' notice before withdrawing. That period would give Israel, the United States and other governments time to reassess Iran's intentions.

Some analysts argue that governments already concerned about Iran's stockpile of 60%-enriched uranium could interpret a withdrawal as a sign that Tehran was moving closer to a nuclear weapons capability.

US-Iran war: Will it ever end? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Bayat said that makes actual withdrawal considerably less attractive than threatening to do so. He added that leaving the treaty could also "complicate Iran's civilian nuclear cooperation."

Membership in the treaty "provides the broader legal and political framework through which non-nuclear states gain access to peaceful nuclear technology," he said. "Russia remains involved in Iran's civilian nuclear sector, particularly at the Bushehr nuclear power plant."

"Formally withdrawing from the treaty could make future cooperation much more difficult politically and legally, even though existing agreements would need to be assessed separately," added Bayat.

Opposition inside Iran

There is no clear consensus in Iran. Rahman Ghahremanpour, a Tehran-based analyst who has written extensively about Iran's nuclear program, told DW that withdrawing from the treaty has been discussed repeatedly but has never become government policy.

"The issue of leaving the NPT is not new and has been raised many times before," he said. "But right now, there are significant legal and political obstacles, and there is still no full consensus within Iran."

Ghahremanpour said the international community would closely examine any attempt to invoke Article X. He points to the ongoing legal debate over North Korea's withdrawal as an example.

North Korea announced its withdrawal from the NPT in 2003. Although Pyongyang is generally treated internationally as no longer being a party to the treaty, some UN documents note that its formal status remains uncertain.

The treaty itself, however, does not require UN Security Council approval for withdrawal. It requires only that states notify the council.

For Ghahremanpour, the political message is more important than the legal process.

He believes talk of leaving the NPT is mainly aimed at pressuring Washington, and particularly European governments, to make concessions.

World.title: Why Starlink won't open Vietnam's heavily censored internet
World.content:
Starlink promises better connectivity in remote and mountainous areas. But in one of Southeast Asia's most tightly controlled online environments, more network access doesn't mean more free speech.

Elon Musk's Starlink has begun selling satellite internet in Vietnam, bringing its high-speed service to one of the world's most tightly controlled online environments.

The satellite internet service operated by Musk's SpaceX began accepting orders from Vietnamese customers this month, with residential packages starting at around €37 ($43) a month.

Vietnam's government announced in March 2025 that it would allow SpaceX to launch Starlink on a controlled trial basis, waiving the usual restrictions on foreign ownership. The trial is capped at 600,000 subscribers and is due to run until the end of 2030.

The service is operated through Starlink Services Vietnam, a local SpaceX subsidiary established last September.

Vietnamese authorities subsequently licensed four ground gateway stations and up to 600,000 Starlink terminals for the initial rollout. The gateways allow satellite traffic to connect with terrestrial telecommunications infrastructure inside Vietnam.

Vietnam authorized the trial in March 2025 as it sought to head off threatened US trade measures over its large bilateral trade surplus.

At the time, some analysts viewed approval of Starlink, alongside tariff reductions on several US products, as part of Hanoi's effort to ease trade tensions with Washington.

Starlink comes at a high cost

Vietnam officially connected to the global internet in 1997. By the end of 2025, it had around 85.6 million internet users, equivalent to 84.2% of the population, according to government data.

Conventional internet infrastructure is already extensive. Around 85% of Vietnamese households had fiber-optic internet, while there were more than 110 million mobile broadband subscriptions, and the country's 5G network covered around 92% of the population, according to official statistics.

Starlink is relatively expensive compared to other network options, but its most obvious advantage is not in well-connected cities such as Hanoi or Ho Chi Minh City but in mountainous, remote and island communities where terrestrial infrastructure remains weaker.

The Vietnamese government says Starlink could help increase internet access in remote areas, islands and places without adequate terrestrial telecommunications infrastructure.

Because satellite connections rely less on local cables and towers, they could also provide backup communications when terrestrial networks are damaged by typhoons, floods or landslides.

However, Starlink currently advertises its cheapest household plan in Vietnam at about €37 a month, while the necessary hardware starts at roughly €284.

In rural areas, where Starlink could potentially be most useful, average monthly income is just €259, according to Vietnam's National Statistics Office.

"Without subsidies, it will be unaffordable for many rural households. Its greatest impact may therefore come through shared connections for institutions such as schools, clinics and local government offices rather than individual subscriptions," Khac Giang Nguyen, a visiting fellow at the ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore, told DW.

Freedom online: Who's negotiating it? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Connectivity without internet freedom

Whatever Starlink does for connectivity, there is little indication that its arrival will loosen Vietnam's increasingly tight control of online speech.

Freedom House's 2025 Freedom on the Net report gave Vietnam a score of just 22 out of 100 and classified the country's internet as "not free." Among the Asia-Pacific countries assessed, only China and Myanmar scored lower.

And foreign technology companies are already central to enforcing those restrictions.

Vietnamese authorities said Facebook, YouTube and TikTok complied with more than 94% of government requests to remove or block content during the first half of 2026.

Human Rights Watch and other rights groups have repeatedly criticized foreign platforms for facilitating state censorship.

In previous years, Hanoi publicly reported compliance rates of around 90% or higher for requests made to Facebook and YouTube to remove content the government considered illegal or anti-state.

The 2025 decision approving the Starlink pilot made clear from the outset that connectivity would remain subordinate to state security concerns, with the telecom ministry stating that the "program will adhere to national security and defense principles," according to the news website VNExpress.

Starlink must play by Vietnam's rules

Vietnam has also steadily expanded the legal tools available to police the internet. Decree 147, which took effect in December 2024, requires social media companies to verify users, hand over certain data and remove content deemed illegal by the authorities within 24 hours.

A new Cybersecurity Law took effect in July, further consolidating state control over cyberspace. New implementing regulations issued on August 19 allow authorities to demand that online content be removed within 24 hours and provide for accounts to be restricted or blocked for repeated violations.

The law also for the first time explicitly refers to constructing a "national firewall" to counter cybersecurity threats.

"As Vietnam is an interesting market for Starlink and the service is on a trial period, the company will ensure that it sticks to the governmental regulations rather than offering the Vietnamese citizens technical options to circumvent censorship," Alfred Gerstl, an expert on Southeast Asia at the University of Vienna, told DW.

Starlink must operate through a Vietnamese company and licensed domestic gateway stations, meaning that its service is not being introduced as a parallel internet infrastructure beyond the reach of Vietnamese regulators.

An analysis by the Singapore Space Agency last month noted that Starlink in Vietnam, unlike in most other Southeast Asian countries, will be channeled through four domestic gateway earth stations and supervised jointly by the Ministry of Science and Technology, the Ministry of National Defense and the Ministry of Public Security.

"Vietnamese instinct is risk containment through enclosure," the report noted.

According to Gerstl, "Starlink will not open a breach in the Bamboo Firewall," a reference to the nickname for Vietnam's system of legal restrictions, content controls and technical measures to regulate the internet.

"The regime will continue to uphold digital sovereignty. Indeed, censorship, currently less strict than in China, is expected to be further expanded in the future," he added.

Starlink may provide Vietnamese users with another way to get online, but it does not provide them with an internet beyond the reach of the Vietnamese state.

At best, said Giang, Starlink may broaden access to information for communities that previously had poor connectivity, which is beneficial in itself, "but better connectivity does not necessarily mean greater freedom of speech," he added.

Bypassing the censors: How to access blocked online content To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

World.title: The US is expanding sanctions on Iran's financial networks. Iranian business owners worry about their economic future
World.content:
The US is expanding sanctions on Iran's financial networks, targeting crypto, gold, aviation and shipping. DW spoke with analysts about what could change.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has unveiled a new phase of Washington's economic campaign against Iran, this time aimed not only at sanctioned Iranian institutions but at the international networks Tehran has used to keep money and goods moving.

Speaking on August 24, Bessent said the United States would target what he called five economic lifelines: digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping. He also warned foreign entities that help the country illicitly move money around.

"Any entity that facilitates money laundering for Iran will be removed from the US dollar-based financial system," Bessent said. "The countdown starts now."

The approach represents an effort to tighten secondary sanctions, putting pressure on companies, financial intermediaries and trading partners outside Iran rather than simply adding restrictions on an economy already heavily sanctioned.

The US announced measures against around 60 individuals, entities and vessels. But it stopped short of targeting major Chinese banks, highlighting the limits of how far the US may be willing to push enforcement against Iran's biggest remaining trading partner.

How Iran has been evading US sanctions

For years, Iran has relied on networks outside the formal banking system to move money.

Exchange houses, gold, cryptocurrency, front companies and opaque shipping networks have helped Iran bypass sanctions.

The latest US strategy appears designed to make those methods more difficult by increasing the cost for foreign intermediaries and comes at a vulnerable moment for Iran.

Though many big-ticket items are priced and sold in US dollars, it would be a stretch to say that Iran's domestic economy has become dollarized Image: Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto/picture alliance

Oil exports have fallen sharply amid US efforts to disrupt Iranian oil shipments. Shipments to China, Iran's main oil customer, dropped to about 534,000 barrels per day in August from 823,000 in July and from a peak of around 1.58 million barrels earlier this year.

At home, food prices rose around 128% year on year in July, according to official data cited by Reuters news agency.

Iran's currency has lost so much value that many transactions, including property and car sales, are now conducted in US dollars. s are sometimes even priced in dollars.

Rising inflation hits Iranian businesses

The pressure is increasingly visible in ordinary businesses.

A building materials seller in the capital, Tehran, told DW that inflation has become so severe that simply holding goods can sometimes be more profitable than selling them.

"If I keep something in my warehouse for a month, its price may rise by more than the profit I would make by selling it today," he said.

He also owns a stone-cutting business and said fulfilling older contracts has become increasingly painful because replacement materials may cost considerably more a few weeks later. And raising prices offers no easy solution.

"If I increase the price beyond a certain point, nobody can afford to buy it," he said.

US troops feel strain of Iran war deployment To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The restrictions also disrupt how private companies pay suppliers, import raw materials and maintain employment.

Another Iranian who works at a trading company told DW that more than 70% of its employees had been laid off during the past six months.

The company imported raw materials for various personal products and previously transferred payments through exchange houses in the United Arab Emirates.

"Now no exchange house is willing to work with us," the employee said.

How sanctions affect Iranian businesses abroad

The effects are also spreading to Iranian businesspeople outside the country.

An Iranian businessman who moved to Dubai told DW that he had previously owned several cosmetics and hygiene brands in Iran. Restrictions on imports and difficulties obtaining raw materials eventually pushed him to relocate.

In Dubai things were more manageable. But since the war, that has changed, he said.

"These days, having an Iranian passport makes almost every transaction more difficult," he told DW.

He said Iranian entrepreneurs are increasingly uncertain whether banks will maintain their accounts or whether residency rules could be tightened.

"In an environment where there is no stability and the outlook is unclear, you cannot really run a business," he said.

Can more sanctions change Tehran's behavior?

Alireza Salavati, a London-based political economy commentator, is skeptical that the new US measures will produce a fundamental strategic shift.

Iran is already sanctioned across most major sectors, he told DW. Further restrictions may involve expanding enforcement of existing networks rather than creating entirely new forms of economic pressure.

"Their principal effects are likely to be psychological, intensifying inflationary expectations," Salavati said.

What if Iran and Oman split control of the Strait of Hormuz? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Salavati also warns that economic pressure could weaken the remaining middle-income and professional groups that traditionally provide space for more moderate politics.

Rather than producing rapid political change, he believes the pressure could deepen polarization and encourage the state to reduce already limited subsidies and social assistance.

Could US sanctions strengthen Iran's shadow economy?

There is another paradox. The more Washington restricts formal financial channels, the stronger the incentive becomes to develop informal ones.

Iran's sanctions economy has already created complex networks of intermediaries, cryptocurrency transfers, front companies, cash transactions and unofficial currency markets.

Closing one route may make transactions more expensive without necessarily stopping them.

"The broader consequence is likely to be corrosive rather than transformative," Salavati said, warning that the result could be an even larger and less controlled underground economy.

The new sanctions may make it harder for Tehran to finance trade, obtain foreign currency and sustain its existing economic networks. But the immediate burden is falling on companies, workers and households already dealing with wartime disruption and extreme inflation.

Whether US pressure changes the behavior of Iran's leadership remains uncertain.

Edited by: Tim Rooks

08/25/2026 August 25, 2026 Strait of Hormuz sees lowest daily vessel count since May

The strait has become a central flashpoint in the war between the United States and Iran Image: REUTERS

Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has fallen sharply, with just two commodity tankers transiting the vital energy chokepoint on Monday, the lowest daily total since early May.

Shipping data from Kpler showed both vessels entered the Gulf, well below the recent daily average of 14 crossings. Some ships may not have been counted after switching off navigation transponders.

Before the conflict, the Strait of Hormuz carried about one-fifth of global crude oil and liquefied natural gas flows.

Iran said it had blacklisted 45 tankers for violating passage rules and threatened action against vessels involved in ship-to-ship transfers with them.

Analysts said it remained unclear how Tehran would enforce those measures, but warned that any escalation or attack in the waterway could further disrupt traffic.

In a sign of how dangerous the crossing can be, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said Monday an oil tanker was hit by an "unknown projectile" off the coast of Oman.

The vessel was disabled but the crew was reported safe. It was not immediately clear who was responsible for the attack.

World.title: Trees are vital for cooler cities, but they need help too
World.content:
Record-breaking heat and drought are putting urban trees at risk. Experts explain how to protect these essential assets and build city forests that can withstand the climate challenges ahead.

Walking beneath the trees this historically hot summer, sometimes felt like autumn had already arrived: dry, dead leaves crunching underfoot, and crowns tinged yellow or completely bare.

That's a problem because large leafy trees help make our cities more livable. They block sunlight, reduce pollution, store carbon, provide habitats for biodiversity to thrive, soak up otherwise harmful stormwater runoff and even boost the mental and physical health of residents.

"When trees go away, those things go away as well," Nina Bassuk, who runs the Urban Horticulture Institute at the US-based Cornell University, told DW.

That's why cities and scientists are racing to figure out how to save trees and choose smarter ones for the future.

Why cities need trees

As humans have burned fossil fuels to power industry and heat homes, the planet has become hotter, making the role of urban trees ever more vital.

Why? Because they essentially act like giant air conditioners, which makes a big difference in hot cities. Inside a tree's canopy, temperatures can be up to three degrees cooler than the surrounding area. This is down to evapotranspiration, the process of trees absorbing water and releasing water vapor through their leaves.

In addition, trees cast shade, which keeps their surroundings from heating up in the first place.

"When we stand under a tree, the temperature we perceive can be 10 to 12 degrees Celsius (18 to 22 degrees Fahrenheit) lower than right next to it," said Matthias Beyer, a hydrologist at the Institute of Geoecology at TU Braunschweig.

And it's not just cooling. There have been numerous studies correlating all sorts of other positive effects of robust trees.

One showed that cities with more tree canopy had lower rates of cardiovascular disease . Another concluded that greener school surroundings were associated with better grades in high schools. And further research suggested that more greenspace exposure during pregnancy can lead to healthier outcomes for newborns.

How much water do trees need to survive drought?

Though a warmer climate makes trees more necessary, it also makes it harder for them to thrive.

Healthy trees need a minimum of 10 to 15 liters of water a day, but mature ones with full foliage require up to four times that.

Different ages of trees require different volumes of water to keep healthy Image: Claus Völker/dpa/picture alliance

While there may be a temptation for cities to focus on planting new, less water-hungry trees, experts agree that the priority should be protecting older, struggling ones.

Research shows it would take around 400 saplings to replace the benefits of an old tree with a crown circumference of 20 meters. Once trees reach maturation, their benefits can be exponential, but this takes time and lots of maintenance.

"A lot of trees can't deliver the full function until 40, 50 years from the day they were planted," said Henrik Sjoman, a researcher at the Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences.

The best way to water trees

It's better to give trees a large amount of water over a short period so it can soak down deep, rather than letting it stay in the upper soil layers, where much of it evaporates.

For newly planted trees, a ring of metal or sturdy plastic is often fixed into the ground around the trunk. Where that's not available, a shallow depression around the tree can be created, allowing the water to pool. What matters is not damaging any surface roots in the process.

When the soil is extremely hardened, so-called irrigation bags or cushions can help. Water drips slowly but steadily into the soil through small holes on their underside. The water mustn't sit on the surface for long periods, since that can cause rot, which damages the tree.

If they don't have the right growing conditions, trees can struggle to put down roots in cities Image: IMAGO/viennaslide

But sometimes the soil has been heavily compacted to support sidewalks above, meaning water can't get through at all. Thirty years ago, Bassuk helped pioneer a method that mixes specially sized gravel in with the soil. It lets the stones bear the load of the sidewalk, while leaving more space for roots to stretch across dense urban ground.

"As long as you get the soil and the stone proportions right, you can compact it and yet trees can access that and grow for long distances," Bassuk said.

How to choose the right trees for cities

When it comes to climate adaptation, there's also the question of which trees to plant in the first place.

Historically, Sjoman says urban tree selection was often driven by aesthetics and design, which led to the over-planting of single species that were vulnerable to threats like pests or disease. Horror stories of Dutch elm disease wiping out entire populations in the 20th century helped to transform urban forestry planning, placing the focus far more on diversity and climate adaptation.

It can take a long time for trees to reach their full potential in terms of how much they can cool their surroundings Image: Philipp Böhme/DW

The 10-20-30 rule of thumb was coined in 1990 by the late Frank Santamour, who worked as a research geneticist at the US National Arboretum. It states that urban forest populations should include no more than 10% of any one species, 20% of a single genus or 30% of any family.

In Germany, there are several tools and databases that offer planting guidance, and several cities are taking part in an official street tree test. The idea is that 45 species are tested at more than 220 locations to gather knowledge of how they thrive.

Another resource is the CITREE database, which categorizes almost 400 species of woody plants, sortable by more than 50 different features, including leaf density, fruit color, allergy potential, limb breakage and more.

The key feature cities need to select is drought tolerance — considering the immense biological strain urban trees are facing in an ever-warming world. But knowing the benefits trees offer a city means that is not the only factor.

"The demands of trees today — it's so much bigger, so much deeper than it was just a couple of decades ago," Sjoman said.



This article was adapted from German, with additional reporting.



Edited by: Tamsin Walker

World.title: Canada set to announce retaliatory tariffs on US goods after talks fail
World.content:
Tariffs of 50% on Canadian goods came into effect after trade talks collapsed. US President Trump has warned Ottawa to "fall in line," but Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has refused to accept a "bad deal."

Canada is set to announce retaliatory tariffs against the United States on Tuesday, as relations between the neighbors nosedived following failed trade talks last week.

Here's what you need to know:

Washington ‌and ​Ottawa were racing to reach an agreement beforeUS President Donald Trump's steep new US tariffs, announced in July, were due to take effect

Talks broke down days after the US President announced the neighbors were close to agreeing to a trade deal

The collapse in negotiations triggered Trump's threatened 50% tariffs on about $20 billion worth of Canadian goods the next day

Canada moved to announce its own retaliatory tariffs effective September 8

Why is Canada imposing new tariffs?

While the US and Canada have shared one of the world’s largest trade relationships, the recent talks signal a breakdown in relations.

"An attitude at the negotiation table that Canada is a subsidiary of the United States" is "not something we’re going to accept," Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said.

"We learned during the negotiations that the Americans want to destroy our major industries, including autos, steel and aluminum," Carney said, opting for an even blunter approach in French. "That was one of the main reasons we said no. It was a bad deal."

US-Canada trade war: The cost of fighting back To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne and three other Cabinet ministers are expected to unveil Canada's response on Tuesday.

What did the US say?

Donald Trump returned to the topic of Canada early on Tuesday on social media, claiming the US was mulling renaming Lake Ontario, the only one of the five North American Great Lakes named after a Canadian territory.

"The United States is giving serious consideration to changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America in that we don't expect to doing [sic] much business with them any longer," Trump wrote.

His administration "renamed" the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America soon after Trump returned to the White House last year — a change that almost nobody besides the US government has implemented. Even US tech giant Google shows it as the Gulf of Mexico first on its maps for users everywhere but in the US.

A day earlier, Trump had threatened he would impose a 50% tariff on Canadian automobiles, car parts and steel from January 1, 2027, and took to social media to unleash a tirade against the historic partner.

Trump hits Canada with 50% tariffs in major trade escalation To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"On trade, ‌and in other ways, also, ‌they ​are among the worst nations in the world to deal with. They feel entitled, and ​yet, WE DON'T NEED CANADA, THEY NEED US!" the US president said.

Canada relies heavily on the US as its top trading partner, with American-bound exports making up 70% of the country's total. The relationship runs both ways, too: government data shows Canada was the second-largest US trading partner in goods this year, just behind Mexico.

No further negotiations are currently scheduled.
