World.title: A second chance: The uncertainty & struggle behind India's organ transplant boom
World.content:
Organ transplant in India. Photo credit: AP

India's organ transplant system works through a three-tier hierarchical network coordinated by NOTTO, ROTTO, and SOTTO

The journey begins before surgery

Live Kidneys lead Indiaâs transplant numbers.

âThe process is not smoothâ

The transplant journey begins long before the operating room, with a long road of tests, paperwork and waiting.

Consent can change the course

Once an organ is allocated, the recipient is prepared for surgery and then closely monitored for complications and organ function

Living donation : another route, but not a simple one

Following the surgery, transplant centres also continue monitoring recipient information and clinical status.

The surgery is only the beginning

The emotional toll of transplantation

Recovery brings a new set of challenges

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

Behind every transplant statistic is a patient who has waited, a donor who has made an extraordinary decision, and a family navigating a system in which every clearance, consent and organ offer can change the course of a life.

Beyond the numbers

Indiaâs transplant system has grown rapidly, from 4,990 transplants in 2013 to 20,138 in 2025. But for a patient, a transplant is far more than a surgical procedure. It is a journey through medical tests, clearances, documentation, waiting, uncertainty, organ matching and, eventually, surgery and lifelong follow-up.Transplant hospitals and coordinators are at the centre of this system, working within the wider network of the National Organ and Tissue Transplant Organisation (NOTTO), Regional Organ and Tissue Transplant Organisations (ROTTOs) and State Organ and Tissue Transplant Organisations (SOTTOs).Yet statistics and institutional structures can obscure what the process actually feels like for the person waiting for an organ. For recipients such as Hemant Kumar Thakur and Shrishti Sinha, the reality is one of uncertainty, exhaustion and fear â followed by the possibility of a second chance at life.A patient with advanced organ failure is first evaluated at a registered transplant centre. The assessment can involve blood tests, imaging, organ-specific investigations and evaluation by a multidisciplinary team. If found medically suitable, the patient is registered in the relevant transplant system.Being on a waiting list, however, does not simply mean waiting in chronological order. Allocation depends on the organ and applicable rules, including factors such as medical urgency, compatibility and, for some organs, time spent on the list. NOTTOâs framework also provides for urgent and super-urgent categories. For kidney patients, for instance, time on dialysis is among the factors considered.NOTTO coordinates the system nationally, while ROTTOs and SOTTOs connect regional and state-level transplant activity. The State Appropriate Authority separately oversees regulatory compliance, including the registration of transplant centres and adherence to legal and ethical requirements.For recipients, however, the elaborate network can feel much simpler: a long wait, a stream of tests and paperwork, and the constant question of what happens next.Hemant Kumar Thakur, from Jamshedpur, Jharkhand, underwent a kidney transplant at Apollo Hospitals in Kolkata, with his wife, Kanchan Mala, donating a kidney. For him, the hardest part was not the operation but navigating the process beforehand.Because he lived in Jharkhand while the transplant took place in West Bengal, Hemant had to deal with inter-state approvals and paperwork.âBecause the procedure involved two different states â Jharkhand and West Bengal â I had to obtain No Objection Certificates (NOCs) from both states before the transplant could proceed,â he said.Despite the difficulties, Hemant was fortunate to have a compatible donor within his family.âThe process is not smooth; it is quite challenging. I was lucky that the match was found within my own family, with my wife,â he said.His experience also made him aware of the uncertainty faced by patients without a matching family donor. He recalled seeing patients who had found donors and completed much of the paperwork, only for the donor to later withdraw.âAfter going through the entire process, they were back where they had started â back to square one,â he said.Indiaâs transplant framework is governed by the Transplantation of Human Organs and Tissues Act, 1994 (THOTA) and related rules. Organ donation must be voluntary and free from commercial dealings, while transplantation is permitted only through authorised institutions.Dr Ankur Garg, GI Surgeon and Liver Transplant Specialist at Paras Health in Gurugram, says legitimate organisations and transplant coordinators play an important role in educating patients, facilitating listing and supporting families when brain-stem death is declared.But he warns that patients can also be targeted by unscrupulous intermediaries.âThere will always be unsocial elements, touts, agents in society luring needy patients and families and giving false hopes and promises of early organ allocation, lesser waiting times and so much extra,â he said.Consent can also change during the donation process. Dr Garg explains that once brain-stem death has been declared and the family consents to donation, the process of identifying eligible recipients begins. But consent can still be withdrawn before organ retrieval.âBefore wheeling into the operation theatre where organ harvesting happens, anyone can withdraw consent, and the whole process will stop,â he said.For recipients, that possibility can mean losing an organ they had been preparing to receive and returning to the uncertainty of the waiting list.Not every patient has to depend on a deceased donor. Certain organs, particularly kidneys and part of the liver, can be donated by living donors after medical, legal and ethical evaluation.The donorâs compatibility and health are assessed, while the legal process depends partly on the relationship between donor and recipient. Near-relative donations follow the applicable framework, while other living-donor relationships may require scrutiny by an Authorisation Committee.Dr Garg says a patient cannot simply register at multiple centres and wait for whichever offers an organ first.âAs per the rule, any patient is allowed to register at one place only. Under NOTTO guidelines and Indian transplant regulations, a patient cannot be registered on a deceased donor waiting list at multiple hospitals or centres simultaneously,â he said.He said the listing process requires a medical summary, blood group, relevant reports and valid Aadhaar or national identification.Once an organ is allocated, the recipient is prepared for surgery and then closely monitored for complications and organ function. But leaving the hospital does not mean leaving the transplant journey behind.Recipients must take prescribed immunosuppressive medicines consistently, attend follow-up appointments and undergo regular investigations. Transplant centres also continue monitoring recipient information and clinical status.Hemant said his own transplant was comparatively smooth once the approvals and paperwork were completed, but the financial and medical commitments continued.He spent approximately Rs 15â20 lakh on the transplant and related treatment in 2020.âI do not have any additional complications. I just go for routine check-ups every six months and have to take medication for the rest of my life,â he said.He currently spends around Rs 7,000â8,000 a month on medicines, although he noted that aftercare and medication costs vary between patients.Hemant also contrasted the long-term experience of the recipient with that of his living donor, his wife.âThe donor has to take medicines for about three months after the transplant and can lead a normal life,â he said.Shrishti Sinha, an engineer who now works as a freelancer in Delhi, describes her transplant journey through a different lens: uncertainty, gratitude, fear and the possibility of rebuilding a future.âThere are many moments of uncertainty. There are medical tests, clearances, waiting for updates and constantly wondering what comes next,â she says.Even hope was fragile.âNot completely. As if one moment hope was rising, the next it was gone. There were cases more severe than mine, or someone who had a higher percentage of surviving,â she recalls.Shrishti underwent treatment at R&R Hospital in Delhi and remembers her doctors as a source of encouragement.âIt was R&R Hospital, Delhi, and the doctors were positive and kept trying to cheer me up,â she says.When she finally realised she would receive an organ, her response was deeply personal.âI was crying and feeling grateful that I was going to live, that I would get to spend more time with my husband and create a future,â she recalls.The transplant did not instantly restore normal life. Shrishti found recovery difficult, from eating and drinking to physiotherapy.âRecovery was not straightforward. There were challenges with eating, drinking and physiotherapy. Seeing the scar for the first time was scary,â she says.There were unexpected experiences, too.âThe weirdest thing was having strange cravings that I never used to have,â she recalls.Five years later, however, she says the biggest change is her ability to think beyond her illness.âThe biggest change is that I can think about the future again. Before the transplant, so much of my life revolved around my health and whether my condition would deteriorate further.âShe now marks the day of her operation as something more than a medical milestone.âFive years later, I have started treating my operation day as my second birthday, a chance to live,â she says.Indiaâs transplant system may be measured in hospitals, registries, waiting lists and annual numbers. But for the person inside it, transplantation is much more intimate: months of paperwork, uncertainty and waiting, followed by surgery and the lifelong responsibility of protecting the new organ.Behind every transplant statistic is a patient who has waited, a donor who has made an extraordinary decision, and a family navigating a system in which every clearance, consent and organ offer can change the course of a life.For recipients like Hemant and Shrishti, the transplant is ultimately not just about surviving. It is about being able to imagine tomorrow again.

World.title: India mulls annual dope tests on all commercial pilots on a random basis

NEW DELHI: Commercial pilots in India could soon be subjected to annual dope tests that may be conducted at random for the surprise factor. After the pilot in command of Air Indiaâs Aug 4 Phuket-Delhi flight had reportedly tested positive, govt had directed the Directorate General of Civil Aviation to review the existing rules for these tests.âThe DGCA is having stakeholder consultation right now on what the current regulation says and how do we ensure there is a strict policy around this (drug tests for pilots) in the future. This consultation is going on right now. There are multiple ways of approaching this dope test. So right now the rule says 10% across the overall pilot network but just like I said DGCA is engaging and one of the opinions from our side is that everyone has to go through it in the year at a random time,â Union aviation minister Ram Mohan Naidu said Tuesday.âWe have to see how all the stakeholders are going to respond to this because one is the safety aspect of to ensure safety intact and the second is the operational impact. That also has to be taken into consideration.. We are going to balance both. If we do 100%, if every pilot has to go through the dope test once a year, then what can happen, what can be the impact of that, that is what DGCA is looking at,â Naidu added.Air India group has initiated a one-time dope test on all its pilots.Other airlines are also doing the same voluntarily, the minister said.The Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (AAIB) is probing the why the Air India Airbus A320 had suffered a sudden loss of altitude by about 300 while operating as AI 2379 on Aug 4 from Phuket to Delhi which had left 20 passengers and four crew members injured. European aerospace major Airbus and Franceâs Bureau of Enquiry and Analysis for Civil Aviation Safety (BEA) also joined the probe under AAIB whose report is expected in a week, according to officials.âBecause everything is intact, the data recorder and everything is intact, the plane has also been in their possessionâ¦So I believe that we can expect some preliminary report very early from now,â Naidu said.

World.title: 2013 rape case: Supreme Court directs Tarun Tejpal to surrender within two weeks
World.content:
NEW DELHI: The

on Tuesday directed former

to surrender within two weeks in connection with the 2013 Goa sexual assault case.

The direction comes after Tejpal challenged the Bombay high court's August 6 judgment, which overturned his acquittal by a trial court and convicted him in the case.

The high court sentenced him to 10 years of rigorous imprisonment.

The Supreme Court's latest direction means Tejpal will have to surrender before serving the sentence, subject to any further orders in his appeal.

The case relates to allegations that Tejpal sexually assaulted a junior colleague inside a hotel elevator in Goa in November 2013 during an event organised by Tehelka magazine.

A Goa sessions court had acquitted Tejpal of all charges in May 2021, holding that the prosecution had failed to establish its case beyond reasonable doubt.

The Goa government challenged the acquittal before the Bombay High Court, which overturned the trial court's verdict on August 6 and convicted Tejpal.

The high court subsequently sentenced him to 10 years of rigorous imprisonment.

Tejpal, through advocate Aditya Samaddar, moved the Supreme Court against the Bombay High Court judgment. The Goa government has also approached the Supreme Court seeking a life sentence, arguing that the 10-year punishment was inadequate considering the nature and seriousness of the offences.
